t: Assertion 3. The Person of the Holy Ghost is not united to the soul of a believer, nor are there two persons here united or made one Spirit by union of person with person; but the person is said to come to the saints, and to dwell with them, and to be in them, Jn. 14:16-17, and God has sent the Spirit of his Son in our hearts, crying ‘Abba Father,’ not that the Holy Ghost, in propper Person, does in us formally and immediately believe, pray, love, repent, etc. we being mere patients in understanding, will, affections, memory, as Libertines teach. But the Holy Ghost comes to the saints and dwelles in them, in the spiritual gifts and saving graces, and supernatural qualities created in us by the Holy Spirit and acted, excited and moved as supernatural and heavenly habits to act with the vital influence of our understanding, will, and affections. I prove the former part: 1. Because such a union of the Person of the Holy Ghost in us, believing, loving, joying, praying and immediately in us, were that blasphemous deifying and Goding of the saints, so as believing, loving, praying were not our works, but the immediate acts of the Holy Ghost, and either the faint manner of believing, or the cold slacked loving, and praying of saints, or their not believing, and sinfull omission of the acts of faith, love, praying rejoicing, could not be more imputed to saints, as their sinful defects and transgressions (but must be laid on the Holy Ghost’s score) than we can impute the splitting of a ship to the ship itself and not to the negligent and willfull pilot who of purpose dashed the vessell on a rock; but we must not in reason blame the ship, but the pilot; for the loss of the ship is the only and proper fault of the man that stirred the ship, and the ship is innocent and harmless timber: Now what sin can be in the saints in these supernaturall acts, if the Holy Ghost immediately in his own Person stir the helm, and only, without us, act these in us? We might with as good reason say the shop that a man works in does make the portrait, which is a great untruth, since the artificer in the shop does it▪ as say that the saints do pray, believe, rejoice, if the Holy Ghost immediately do all these in them, as in a shop. 2. Upon the same ground the Lord’s coming down and filling John Baptist from his mother’s womb, and the apostles and Steven full of the Holy Ghost, should be the Holy Ghost’s personal filling of them, and his immediate acting in them, without any action of them in preaching, praying, and their heavenly bold confessing of Christ before men; and there should be no difference between the ark and temple of Jerusalem, filled with the immediate presence of God, in the Lord’s manifestation of his glory there, and these saints filled with God, in these works of free grace. I shall not believe that the person of God can be said to be united to either ark, temple, apostle or martyr; all the union is in the effects and manifestations of graces, or tokens of divine presence, which are creatures rising and falling with time. 3. That excellent and living ark, the most glorious and admirable thing that heaven has, the Lord Jesus, is God and man, two naturee united in one person. But both the Word of God making that He▪ that same Holy thing, born of the virgin Mary, the Son of God, Lk. 1:5, and that same He, and Person who came of the Jews, according to the flesh, to be God blessed forever, Rom. 9:5; Heb. 7:3; Mt. 16:13, 16, and the third general council, called that of Ephesus, and after the council of Chalcedon, ver. 4 and 5, do evidence to us that Christ cannot be two persons as Nestorius dreamed, and one person. Paul spread the Gospel from Jerusalem to Iliricum, about ten hundred miles. I know not he, but the grace of God that was with him, 1 Cor. 15:9-10, not he, but the Lord: True, but the question now is whether Paul and the Holy Ghost in all these works of grace, were two persons become one Spirit by union, as some dreamers affirm; because both did the work; I believe not: God and cloud rained down manna to Israel; O but Christ’s Father, Jn. 6, gave the manna, but the question is if the person of God were united with the clouds or any second causes producing manna; so the Lord ‘makes rich and poor, kills and makes alive, makes snow, frost, fair weather,’ drought and rain, the sun to rise, and go down, and that in his own person, Father, Son, and Spirit; He, He only made heaven, earth, sea, and all creatures, and the world; [Greek] Acts 17:25 and [Hebrew] Ps. 33:9, do prove Him to be a person who does all these. But we cannot say that the person of God must be united with clouds, ship, sea, sun, heavens, men fighting and men saving and killing; and that God personally fills all creatures, only God in the immensity of his nature, is all these and everywhere, and is in them by his operation; so the Holy Ghost is with the saints and dwells in 〈◊〉, not by union of his Person to them or the immensity of his essence, which is, as David says, everywhere, Ps. 139:7… But He dwells in the saints, in regard of the works, operations, gifts and graces of the Holy Ghost. 1. Because the Holy Spirit is in them, in that they have in them the fruits of the Spirit, Gal. 5.22, such as love, joy, peace, long-suffering, gentleness, goodness, faith; now these are not the Holy Ghost, who is eternal and God uncreated, but are created in time, out of mere nothing, not out of the potency of the subject, but ere God produce grace, so knotty and so rocky are we, and so contrary to grace, that he must fall upon a new and second creation, Eph. 2:10; Col. 2:10; Ps. 51:10, the same word that is used for creating heaven and earth, Gen. 1.•. is here used; it is not like the repairing of a fallen house, where the same timber and stones may do the work, or the repairing of decayed nature, when a healthy body recovers out of a fever; Grace is a rare and curious workmanship. 2. We are said to grow in grace, 2 Pet. 3.18, and by grace to increase to the edifying of the body in love, Eph. 4:16, and to the measure of the stature of the fullnesse of Christ, 13, and to add grace to grace, 2 Pet. 1:5-7, and to go on to perfection, Heb. 6:1; Phil. 3:12. But the person of the Holy Ghost, is not capable of growing, or addition, nor like the morning light, or the new moone, that can grow and advance in perfection, being God blessed forever. 3. If there be a union of the Person of the Holy Ghost with the soul, and not an indwelling by graces, the believer as a believer must live by the uncreated and eternall life of the Holy Ghost, or a created life. Creatum vel increatum dividunt omne ens immediate, sicut finitum et infinitum: Not the former, neither any man, nor the man-Christ can in any capacity be elevated so above itself as to partake of the infinite life of God; how the manhood of Christ partakes of the personal subsistence of the Godhead is incomprehensible to me, except that it is not by such a union as my singular nature stands under personality created, and [it] is by assumption rather than union; however, if there be a union of the Person of the Holy Ghost to our souls, it cannot be conceived, nor does Scripture speak of it; if the saints live the life of God, it must be by created graces, and this is that [which] we conceive. 4. The person of the Holy Ghost immediately acting in the saints, without them or any active and vital influence of the natural faculties, cannot be guilty of sin, because David and Christ are absolved of sin in this: ‘They laid to my charge things that I knew not,’ that is, things I never acted, crimes in which I had no action or hand: but we are blamed in the Word for all the omissions of holy duties; and the Holy Ghost cannot be blamed, for He blows when and where He lists, and is under no Law in his motions of free grace; then he who cannot be blamed in not acting, cannot be united as one spirit, person with person, with him who is justly to be blamed in not acting. Assertion 4: It must evidently follow that there is in the saints a grace created that is neither Christ, nor the Holy Ghost in person; for what reason any has to fancy an union of the person of Christ or the Holy Ghost in the saints [as one person], the same reason have they to say that all the three are united to the person of the believer in all supernatural actions, for the Father is said to draw men to the Son, John 6:44, and Christ to reveal the Father, and to draw men, John 1:18; John 12:32 and the Holy Ghost to reveal the deep things of God, 1 Cor. 2:10-11, now all the three in person do these, but all the three persons are not united to believers in person; this were a mystery greater then God manifested in the flesh, and unknown to Scripture. 2. If Christ be all the grace of believers, faith in Christ and the love of Christ should be Christ. 3. Then should a believer having a new heart, and a new Spirit, be Christed, or Godded; and God should be incarnate in every believer, and how many Christ’s should there be? and the new heart in one saint, and the grace given to Paul, should be the new heart given to Peter, whereas God has given grace to every man according to his measure, and there are diversity of gifts, but one Spirit, 2 Pet. 3:15; Phil. 1:9; Eph. 3:3-5; 1 Cor..12.3-6; Eph. 4:16.
w: Christ Dying & Drawing Sinners to Himself

t: The distortion of double predestination looks like this: There is a symmetry that exists between election and reprobation. God works in the same way and same manner with respect to the elect and to the reprobate. That is to say, from all eternity God decreed some to election and by divine initiative works faith in their hearts and brings them actively to salvation. By the same token, from all eternity God decrees some to sin and damnation (destinare ad peccatum) and actively intervenes to work sin in their lives, bringing them to damnation by divine initiative. In the case of the elect, regeneration is the monergistic work of God. In the case of the reprobate, sin and degeneration are the monergistic work of God. Stated another way, we can establish a parallelism of foreordination and predestination by means of a positive symmetry. We can call this a positive-positive view of predestination. This is, God positively and actively intervenes in the lives of the elect to bring them to salvation. In the same way God positively and actively intervenes in the life of the reprobate to bring him to sin. This distortion of positive-positive predestination clearly makes God the author of sin who punishes a person for doing what God monergistically and irresistibly coerces man to do. Such a view is indeed a monstrous assault on the integrity of God. This is not the Reformed view of predestination, but a gross and inexcusable caricature of the doctrine. Such a view may be identified with what is often loosely described as hyper-Calvinism and involves a radical form of supralapsarianism. Such a view of predestination has been virtually universally and monolithically rejected by Reformed thinkers.

t: V. The subscriptio [to the letter to the Colossians] indicates the ministerial cause through which the Holy Spirit, as the author and primary authority, has used this epistle. That [ministerial] cause is Paul. VI. It is described by the added clause, namely that he is an Apostle of Jesus Christ, that is, an Ambassador and Teacher of the Church, immediately taught by Christ Himself through revelation and sent to proclaim the Gospel of the Messiah exhibited everywhere in the whole world and to establish the foundation of the Church, having this testimony from God, that he has not erred in doctrine.

t: There is one of the chief Reformed divines, Dr. Alting, who in his Problematical Theology, part. 2, problem 21, puts this question: Utrum Judaei in societate Christianorum tolerandi sint [Whether Jews are to be tolerated in the society of Christians]? And he does answer it affirmatively; and I am clearly of his opinion, that it is not only lawful, but if matters be rightly ordered towards them, expedient to admit of them; Nay to invite and encourage them to live in Reformed Christian commonwealths. How far it may be a sin to refuse them admittance when they do desire it upon lawful terms and in a reasonable way, is a further question, which cannot be decided, till the former points of the lawfulness and expediency of admitting of them be made out.
w: ‘A Case of Conscience: Whether it be Lawful to Admit Jews into a Christian Commonwealth?’

t: It was a saying of Martin Luther, Se propter unum Judaeum crucifixum omnibus favere Judaeis [Due to one crucified Jew, there is favor to all the Jews]. And if we love them and desire their conversion and salvation (as in Christian charity certainly we ought), then the way to effect that will not be to banish them and prohibit their habitation amongst us, so compelling them to live amongst Turks, Pagans or Papists; The images and idolatry of which last has undeniably been the greatest scandal, and Remora, which has long hindered them from being Christians. Whereas (if they be permitted to live amongst us) that stumbling-block will be taken away. 2. For the conditions of their admission, for the restrictions and limitations to be put upon them, a great deal of caution and Christian prudence is to be used, lest while we pretend their good we do mischief to ourselves. For as to deny them all liberty and commerce with us, may be an act of unchristian and indeed inhumane cruelty; So to give them too much is an act of imprudence and folly. And indeed we find some sober men (not without good reason) complain of the too much liberty they have in some Christian commonwealths. In short, what qualifications and limitations are to be put upon them, I shall not take upon me to determine, but leave that to the piety and prudence of the State. Yet (with submission) I conceive such limitations as these will be convenient, if not necessary; the rather because I find in our histories, in the imperial and canon laws, and in the old capitulars and canons of councils that such restrictions have been anciently laid upon them, as: 1. No toleration ever was, or de jure can be given them to profess or practice anything against the Law of Nature. 2. No toleration should be given them to speak anything blasphemously or impiously against Jesus Christ and the gospel: For though we may tolerate them in the profession of a bad, yet not in that blasphemy of a good, religion. 3. They never were nor should be permitted to circumcise children of Christians, or seduce any Christians to their religion: Let them profess, but not propagate their religion. 4. They were not permitted to carry any office or dignity in the Christian commonweal, though it seems that sometimes even that was permitted them. 5. They were not permitted in any suit or difference between a Jew and a Christian to draw the Christian or his Cause before a Jewish magistrate: For ’tis a ruled case in the Imperial Law, Judaeus Actor vel reus, Forum sequitur Christianum. 6. They were never permitted to make marriages with Christians, and the Glossator gives the reason of it in Law, Quia matrimonium debet esse communicatio divini & humani juris. Whereas a Jew and Christian, being of different religions, cannot communicare in sacis. And this is consonant to the Law of the Gospel, which forbids us to be unequally yoked. Upon which grounds, I believe all marriages with Papists to be unlawful, that is, Fieri non debuit, ’tis unlawful to make such matches, though that factum valet, when such a match is made, the contract is valid. 7. Their frequent divorcing their wives was tolerated. For though Moses seem to suffer it, yet the emperors by express edict forbid it. 8. By the Imperial Laws polygamy and plurality of wives was not tolerated in them. 9. If any of the Jews turn Christian (by civil law) in case the Jews endeavored to reduce him, and maliciously injured him, they were to be burned for it. 10. They might repair their old synagogues, but were not tolerated (by the Roman Laws) to build new. 11. They were not tolerated to have any Christian servants, nurses, or midwives. Can. Praesenti. 1. Extra de Judaeis. Ex concilio malis conenti. 12. By the Canon Law they might not come abroad on Good Friday. 13. They were not permitted to wear Garments exactly of the Christian fashion, but were to have distinct habits [garments], that all might know them to be Jews. 14. They might not be physicians or give physick to any Christian. 15. They were not permitted to be of the Roman militia (though they were permitted to be advocates) by the rescript of Honorius and Arcadius to Romulianus P. P. 16. The Jews, being the greatest usurers in the world, and believing they may justly take the highest use they can get (even Usurae centessimae, if they could have it) of us gentiles, it is all the reason in the world they should be limited in this particular and not permitted to take more of us than the law permits us to take one of another. 17. They should be enjoined to admit of friendly collations and disputations sometimes about gospel truths, and not obstinately to reject all means of conversion and conviction, and satisfaction of those seeming reasons which keep them off from embracing the truth: For there will be little hopes (or possibility) of their conversion, if they be permitted obstinately to refuse all means of doing it. But enough (if not too much) of this, I shall only add one old law concerning the Jews made before the Conquest (above 600 years ago) and confirmed by the conquerors amongst other the good laws of Edward the Confessor, and so continued law (for ought I know) in all the kings’ reigns till the banishment of the Jews, which was anno 18 Edwardi 1. The Law is this: Sciendum quoque quod omnes Judaei, ubicunque in Regno sunt, sub tutela et defensione Regis ligea debent esse; nec quilibet eorum alicui Diviti se potest subdere, sine Regis licentia. Judaei enim, et omnia sua Regis sunt, Quod si quisquis detinuerit eos, vel Pecuniam eorum, perquirat Rex si vult, tanquam suum proprium. [It should also be known that all Jews, wherever they are in the kingdom, ought to be under the protection and defense of the king’s liege authority; nor may any one of them submit himself to any rich man without the king’s permission. For the Jews, and everything belonging to them, are the king’s. And if anyone detains them, or their money, the king may recover it if he wishes, as his own property.] I wish the chief magistrate could admit them on these terms, for so they, and all theirs (omnia sua) should be suum proprium, which possibly might supply him with money and so save taxes. And upon these terms I (and I believe everybody else) will willingly consent to their readmission.

t: “46. Now there remains to speak somewhat particularly of Jews and heretics: for this kind of men are suffered almost in all cities, provinces and kingdoms, and they dwell together with Christians. Why the Jews should be suffered, Augustine among others brings certain reasons. He, Of the City of God, bk. 4, ch. 18, as also upon the 58th psalm and in other places, writes that therefore they be suffered because they before other men had the promise of salvation; neither are they past all hope, seeing that some of them many times, although few in number, do return unto Christ. ‘Blindness’ (says Paul unto the Romans) ‘fell partly upon Israel’ (Rom. 11:25): as though he would say not upon all. And to this the same apostle adds, ‘When the fulness of the gentiles is come in, then all Israel shall be saved.’ (Rom. 11:25-26) And lest peradventure thou shouldest think that these words are spoken allegorically, Paul writes them as a mystery. And to prove his saying he brings the prophecy of Isaiah the prophet, to wit, that ‘the iniquity shall be then taken away from Jacob.’ Furthermore, they be now called ‘enemies unto God for our sakes, but friends in respect of their fathers.’ The same Augustine, in his Questions upon the Gospel, bk. 2 and question 33 (if those be Augustine’s books) when he interprets the parable of the prodigal son, he says that that son does betoken the gentiles. For it is written, that he departed into a far country (Lk. 15:11); because the ethnics were so far departed from God as they worshipped idols publicly and in open profession. But the elder son, under whom is shadowed the Hebrew people, went not so far off. And although he were not within his father’s house, which is the church, yet nevertheless he abode in the field. For the Jews are occupied in the holy scriptures, which they understand not rightly, nor with such spiritual sense as the church of Christ does know them; but take them in an earthly and carnal manner, whereby not unaptly they be said to have their abode in the field. This elder son does not at the beginning enter into his father’s house, but in the latter days he shall also be called and come. 47. The same father also for the proof of this doctrine brings that which is written in the 59th psalm, as he reads it, ‘Do not kill them, lest they forget thy law, but scatter them in thy power.’ (v. 12) The Son of God (says he) prays unto the Father that the same nation might not be destroyed, but that it might wander every where in the world. Other provinces, when they were overcome of the Romans, followed the laws and rites of the Romans, so that at length they became Romans: but the Hebrews, notwithstanding they were overcome by the Romans, yet would they never yield unto their laws, rites and ceremonies. They still observe their own as much as they may; and being dispersed, they wander abroad. Neither have they utterly forgotten the law of God; not that the godly apply themselves to observe it, but do only read it and keep certain rites and ceremonies, whereby they are discerned from other nations. Verily it seems that God has put a sign upon them as He did upon Cain for killing his brother Abel, namely, that every man should not kill them. (Gen. 4:15) Neither is this scattering of them abroad in the world unprofitable unto the Christians, because (as it is written to the Romans) they are showed unto us as broken boughs. (Rom. 11:17) And for so much as we were grafted in their place, when as we see that they were so miserably cut off, we acknowledge the grace of God towards us: and by beholding of them be taught to take heed that for our infidelity’s sake, for the which they were broken off, we also be not cut off in like manner. Moreover, there is another commodity which comes unto us by the dispersing of them. Because our books are saved by them; I mean the holy Bible, which they carry everywhere about them and read it. And although because they be blinded they believe not, yet they confess that those writings are most true. Indeed they be in heart our deadly enemies; but yet by these books, which they have and reverence, they are a testimony to our religion. Wherefore I cannot marvel sufficiently at those which do so much hate the Jewish tongue and Bibles in Hebrew, as they desire to have them destroyed and burnt, seeing Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, thinks, that wheresoever we doubt of the Greek or Latin translation, we must flee unto the truth of the Hebrew. And Jerome in many places writes the same. 48. But they say that the holy books were abused and corrupted by the Hebrews. To this Jerome upon Isaiah, the sixth chapter, towards the end, answers thus: Either they did this before the coming of Christ and the preaching of the apostles, or else afterward. If a man will say that it was done of them before, then, seeing Christ and his apostles reprehended the most grievous wicked acts of the Jews, I marvel why they would say nothing of that sacrilege and so detestable a wicked act. Undoubtedly they would have reproved them for marring and corrupting of the scriptures. But if thou wilt affirm that the faults were brought in by them afterward: then will I say that it had behooved them to corrupt those places chiefly which do testify of Christ and of his religion; and which were alleged by the Lord Himself and his apostles in the New Testament. But those places remain sound; and the very same sentences which they cited do remain still in the Hebrew Bibles: for they were not so greatly careful for the words, and it is not likely, that they in other places have corrupted the holy scriptures. Yea, if a man diligently read over their books, he shall find in them a great many more testimonies, and those more plain and manifest, than our common translation has. Do they not read in the second psalm, ‘Kiss the son’: which our men have translated, ‘Take ye hold of discipline?’ Which words undoubtedly are referred unto Christ. But I do not mean at this present to bring all such like testimonies: it is sufficient if I prove with Jerome that the books of holy scriptures are not corrupted by the Hebrews. The which surely, if they would have done, yet had they missed of their purpose. For many of the most ancient books are found, and that in written hand, which have been kept a very long time by the Christians, which never came in their hands to abuse. 49. But let us return to discourse of that commodity, which Augustine has declared; There be very many (says he) which would peradventure think that the things which we affirm to be done of the ancient people and of the prophets were but vain and imagined by us, unless they saw the Jews yet alive, who with their books maintain that which we profess, whether they will or no. For although the Hebrews be blinded in their heart, and be against us with as much power as they can, yet we have themselves, together with their books, most evident testimonies of our religion. And doubtless, among all testimonies, that testimony is of greatest account, which is testified by the enemies. And of this kind of witnesses God has provided great store for his Church: for we not only have the Hebrew books to make on our side, but also the verses of the Sibyls, which were born in sundry countries. Neither must it be thought, that those verses were invented by our forefathers themselves: for in the time of Lactantius, Eusebius of Caesaria and Augustine, which alleged those verses, the books of the Sibyls were rife in every man’s hand. So as, if they had added any counterfeit verses unto them, the ethnics, which were then many in number and were full of eloquence, and deadly enemies unto our religion, would have reproved them as vain and lying. What then remains but that God would wonderfully defend his Church even by the testimonies of his adversaries? Now then, the Jews are tolerated among the Christians, partly for the promise’s sake, which they have of salvation to be given to their kindred, and partly because of the commodities, which I have now recited out of Augustine. Wherefore they be not only borne withal, but they have also synagogues where they openly read the books of the holy scripture and one with another do call upon the God of their fathers. In which thing nevertheless, the diligence of magistrates and bishops is to be required, who ought to provide that they do nothing else there, and by all means to beware that in their public prayers, exhortations and sermons they do not curse nor rail upon Christ our God. And this, if our magistrates and bishops do not look unto, they cannot escape a just accusation. But it is not lawful to grant unto the Turks any religious assemblies, for that they have not any particular promise of their salvation: neither would they read there either the Old Testament or the New, but only their most detestable Al Koran. Over this, the Jews should be prohibited to exercise false bargaining and usury among Christians, thereby to vex and afflict the poor Christians before our face: the which cannot be done without great indignity. But our princes exact a good, great tribute of them; and of those gains which come by usury and naughty bargaining, they obtain great prey: so far are they from forbidding them these evil arts. Furthermore (a thing no less hurtful), they provide not to have them taught, when as they ought to compel them to come often to godly Christian sermons: otherwise, while they be so negligently left, they become daily worse and worse. Whereby, either naughty fruit or in a manner none at all can be looked for by the conversation which they have among Christians. It must also be looked diligently to that they corrupt not Christians in seducing them to their Jewish religion. By reason of neglecting hereof, the heresy of the Marrans has much increased, specially in Spain. Moreover, it is meet that they may by some apparel or certain token be known from Christians, lest any unwittingly should be familiar with them no less than with the Christians. And these things shall suffice concerning this sort of infidels.

t: Whether Jews should be tolerated in the society of Christians? The horrendous judgments of God exercised upon the Jews on account of their ingratitude and incredulity were not only set forth long ago in the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, the slaughter of the whole nation and the destruction of the Mosaic Polity: but they also remain before our eyes to this very day. For we see them living dispersed among all nations throughout almost the entire world, subject to the empires of others hard and unjust, to be objects of contempt and scorn to all, and to be treated no otherwise than as slaves or chattels, as much by Christians as by Mahometans and other infidels: finally, not to be received by some and to be expelled by others who had already received them and tolerated them for a long time: in some places, they even barely redeem passage or safe conduct through provinces for the sake of making a journey with a great sum of money. Certainly, in previous centuries, they were excluded from all of France at once and together, no less than the Templars. Similarly, they are exiled from all of Britain. Rupert the Elder, Count Palatine, for I know not what reason, expelled the Jews not only from Heidelberg, but also from the entire Palatinate: and he donated their synagogue, which has now been converted into a Medical Auditorium, and most of the buildings to the Academy, which he founded not long after. And it is known what has been plotted against them in these recent years, partly in Frankfurt, partly in Worms. Nor are there lacking specious reasons by which it is usually persuaded that they are not to be tolerated: They are, they say, enemies of God and Christ, blasphemers. They are enemies of Christians, usurers, money-lenders, who afflict and suck dry the poor. They are also traitors who betray the secrets of Christians to the Turks and others of this kind. On the contrary, there are also found those who undertake the patronage of the Jews, and either tolerate them or receive them anew, or even persuade that they ought to be received and tolerated: but some are led by the hope of profit or gain which they receive from the Jews: others are impelled by a zeal for charity and their conversion. Therefore, so that it may be clear what ought to be decided or followed here, I shall submit an explanation of the problem constructed from the Word of God. I premise, however, two theorems, necessary to be observed. One, that the Jews ought to be considered by us in four ways. They are to be viewed: I. as men, participants of the same flesh and blood as we are, and sprung from the same parent, Adam. II. as descendants of Abraham, as the firstborn of the family of God. In which respect the apostle does not hesitate to call the Jews of his time, although senseless, rebellious and unbelieving, nevertheless ‘saints’: by reason of the fathers, that is, of the firstfruits and the root, from which the lump and the branches are considered sanctified. (Rom. 9:3-5; 11:16) III. as enemies of Christ and the true Church, blasphemers, infidels, money-lenders, usurers: for which reasons they are the offscourings [καθάρματα] of the world, and the public hatred of the whole orb. IV. That they are to be converted to the faith of Christ, according to the grace of predestination and the promise of the eternal Covenant, initiated with Abraham: and indeed [they are to be converted] in great number and multitude. Which conversion, as a mystery divinely revealed to him, the apostle proposes in Rom. 11, verse 25 and following, and confirms it clearly, partly by reasons, partly by the testimonies of the prophets. The other point: That those four modes of consideration ought to be viewed by us not separately, or individually one by one, but all of them conjunctively. When therefore it is asked, whether the Jews are to be tolerated among Christians, one must not judge separately from the third mode, in which they are said to be enemies of Christ, infidels, usurers, but one must pronounce simultaneously also from the others, and especially from the second and fourth: in which they are called the seed of Abraham, to be converted to Christ and to be brought back to the society of the Covenant. This is the reason: because the apostle speaks and judges of them in that way and no other. Rom. 11, verse 16, ‘For if the firstfruits are holy, the lump is also holy; and if the root is holy, so are the branches.’ Likewise verse 28: ‘they are enemies for your sake, but beloved for the sake of the fathers.’ According to these things we now answer affirmatively: namely, that the Jews are to be tolerated in the society of Christians. These are the reasons: First: Although God imposed upon them the punishment of dispersion, so that without a king, scepter and civil law they live scattered among other nations throughout almost the whole world: yet He preserves them wonderfully, nay even miraculously, so that they are not destroyed, nor can they be destroyed, although it has been attempted by many: nor are they even confounded with other nations, in rites, ceremonies, marriages, and the custom of their whole life. And as Cain was marked divinely with a sign, lest he should be killed by those he met on account of fratricide: so the Jews seem to be marked by God on their faces and foreheads, on account of the slaughter of Christ the firstborn, so that they can be recognized almost at first glance, lest they be killed. Therefore, those who do not wish to tolerate the Jews seem to oppose the counsel of God. Second: The dispersion of the Jews throughout the Christian world is useful to us Christians: and that in two ways: I. On account of the spectacle of the severity and wrath of God, which ought to be kept perpetually before our eyes. For they are shown to us as branches broken off on account of unbelief, so that through faith we may learn to remain in the true olive tree, Rom. 11:22 ff. II. On account of the testimony of sound doctrine, which they carry about in the Scriptures of the O.T.: so that the Church may everywhere find witnesses of the Christian religion, as Augustine teaches, Of the City of God, bk. 18, ch. 46. And this testimony is so much the firmer because it is borne to the doctrine by the very enemies, and indeed sworn ones, of it. Therefore the fathers called the Jews the librarians of the Christians, enemies in their hearts, witnesses in their books. Hence, lest we be an obstacle to ourselves, we ought to bear with the Jews in our society. Third, from the examples of the apostles: Peter and Paul showed the highest charity to those very Jews who had driven the Lord Jesus to the cross although they had heard his doctrine with their own ears and had beheld his miracles with their own eyes; and who, having corrupted the witnesses of his glorious resurrection with money, were even much more detestable than the Jews of today; and they did not hesitate to seek and procure their conversion by all means, even at the expense of their own safety: so far were they from being unwilling to tolerate them, Acts 2-3; Rom. 9. Therefore it is much more fitting for us to do the same regarding the Jews of today. Fourth: The Jews, according to the doctrine of the apostle, Rom. 11, are again to be converted to Christ and to faith in Him. But since this cannot be done by infidels, who themselves are ignorant of Christ and do not receive Him, but must be done by the ministry of Christians and the faithful, they certainly ought to dwell and converse among them. Fifth: The Apostle teaches that not only are the Jews to be converted in the greatest number, but also the manner of conversion: which he establishes in this, that they be provoked to emulation, Rom. 11:11, that is, that by the example of the faithful from the gentiles, they themselves also may desire and embrace the grace of Christ. If the Jews are to be provoked to emulation by us, by our example, they certainly ought to be tolerated by us and to dwell among us. From this, however, we further gather two things: I. That the Jews ought to dwell among Evangelicals and Orthodox rather than among Papists. Reason: because the latter are less fit to excite emulation in them: since they are idolaters, whom they [the Jews] turn away from and execrate with their whole heart. II. That conversion of all Israel, or of the Jews in the greatest number, of which the apostle prophesies in Rom. 11, will without doubt follow immediately upon the ruin of the Papacy, and the destruction of the city of Rome, since Papism is the chief obstacle and greatest impediment to the conversion of the Jews to Christianity, which they almost measure by that idolatrous Papism. Sixth. If all Christian magistrates were to exclude the Jews from the society of Christians, and would no longer tolerate them; they would certainly have to be relegated to the Garamantes and Indians, to the Caribs and Cannibals, so that they might spend their lives among them. But in that way, it would surely be poorly provided for them regarding teachers, who might show them the way to find the Messiah whom they seek. We conclude, therefore, that the Jews are to be tolerated among Christians. Furthermore, since it is acknowledged that the Jews, according to the third consideration are not only infidels, but also blasphemers against Christ, enemies of Christians, and most iniquitous usurers, their toleration must be circumscribed by certain conditions as if by certain laws. Here, therefore, some things must be avoided and shunned by Christian magistrates, and other things, on the contrary, must be done: Those things must be avoided which, on account of usury and participation in it, [countries] either admit or tolerate Jews—which, alas, is excessively common today in Germany and elsewhere. Furthermore, these things must be done and cared for by Christian magistrates: I. That the Jews in their synagogues and sacred assemblies should only read the Holy books of the Old Testament and call upon the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob according to the Scripture of the Old Testament. II. That they should take care that they be instructed in the Christian religion and taught about it: indeed, that they even compel them to attend the sacred sermons of the Christians from time to time. For otherwise they can neither be provoked to emulation nor converted to the faith of Christ. And the neglect of this admonition is perhaps the primary reason why so few Jews are converted today. III. That they also accustom and lead them to honest labors and honest crafts: so that they may thus be able to sustain life honestly, even without usury. IV. That they provide them with the security and defense due to all citizens living according to the Laws: and that they do not allow them to be vexed with impunity by the injuries of private individuals, whether publicly or privately. Which is also, alas, too much in use! It is, however, against the apostle, who gravely forbids us Christians from injuries, insults and contempt of the Jews. V. That they ensure that the Jews are distinguished from Christians by their dress or by some certain sign, so that no one through ignorance may associate with them just as they would with Christians. In sum, Christian princes and magistrates who have received or are receiving Jews into their protection, shall show, both in these and in all other things, that they are moved to that [protection] by nothing other than holy charity and a desire to procure their salvation: and therefore they will permit them nothing that is in itself illicit: they will take care that they be instructed in the Christian faith and truth: so that they may thus be able to be salutary instruments in that work which God promised He would do through the prophet Isaiah and the apostle Paul. This much concerning the problem itself.

Whether the Jews be to be tolerated by the Christian magistrate, and how they are to be handled? (System Controvers. Theolog. quae Christianis cum Judaeis intercedunt, Elench. Jud. 8 et ult. Profecto excusari Magistratus Christianus non potest, si impune eorum blasphemias horrendas in Christum, et S.S. Trinitatem, totamque religionem Christianam, diutiùs oculo connivente toleret. [Certainly, the Christian magistrate cannot excuse himself if he should tolerate, with his eye winking, their horrible blasphemies against Christ, the most holy Trinity, and the whole Christian religion, with impunity, for a longer time.”] Idem, ibid. Amongst Gregory’s Epistles, there is one De Judaeis non persequendis [That the Jews are not to be persecuted].) He says it is a perplex[ed] question by reason of the different judgments. He propounds: First, diverse arguments of those which hold they are altogether to be cast out of a Christian commonwealth by reason of those horrible blasphemies which daily, both in their ordinary prayers and in their speeches they belch out against Christ, the Virgin Mary, our Faith, and all Christians in general, and for other reasons which he there alleges. Secondly, He urges other arguments to prove that the Jews are not to be cast out, but tolerated under the Christian magistrate, because by that means many of them may be converted by continual converse with the Christians, and the Scripture seems evidently to confirm that, Hos. 3:4; Zeph. 3:7; Lk. 21:24; Rom. 11:25-26, and because they may be serviceable to them against the pagans and for other reasons. He himself goes the middle way and lays down his opinion in certain propositions: First, It is better for Jews to live amongst Christians than under Turks or infidels. Secondly, The blasphemies of Jews are not to be tolerated, but to be prohibited and most severely punished by Christians. Thirdly, the Jews are to be esteemed among Christians as the servants of servants, that is so to be handled that they are exiles and cast off by God Himself. They are not to have any public office. They are not to practice that unjust usury for which they are so infamous amongst Christians. They are to have also (said he) some outward mark in their garments, by which they may be distinguished from others, and [are] to be forced to hear sermons. Many other cautions does he give in the receiving of them. As for the toleration of the Jews, whosoever they be that suffer the exercise of their religion with the blasphemies they commonly use against Christ, make themselves guilty of all their wickedness, which the Lord keep this land from, as well as from the abomination of the Mass. The Pope can tolerate the blasphemy of the Jews and the filthiness of all the courtesans and stews, and take a yearly rent of them for it, and for no respect will allow the exercise of our most holy religion either in his own dominions or wheresoever he may prevail against us. t: §17. Now to the Political Means. I. Nothing is accomplished, indeed, things are done badly, by persecuting, harassing or oppressing the Jews, driving them away, or killing them. That is to say, those guilty of Judaism alone [should not be harassed or oppressed]. But those guilty of other crimes should be punished equally with others. Nevertheless, they should not be treated more harshly for that reason, because they are Jews. We do not wish innocent people to be constrained merely because they are Jews or Saracens. Among the ancient Sicilian laws, Emperor Frederick established this in Constitutions of Sicily, bk. 1, title 17 & 26: ‘We cannot allow Jews and Saracens, whom the diversity of the Christian sect makes hostile, and who are deprived of every other assistance, to be defrauded of the power of our protection.’ Christian converts from Judaism have noted that this perverse practice of treating Jews more harshly is a great hindrance to the conversion of more people. For it is entirely foreign to the nature of faith to employ violence in order to produce belief. Petrus Alphonsus the Spaniard, in The Dialogue of Moses & Peter: ‘To imprison and kill, until someone either believes or pays a tax, is not among the works of God; nor did any of the prophets command anyone to be compelled to believe.’ Likewise, Stephanus Isaacus (to whom, together with his father Johannes Isaacus, Cardinal and Papal Legate Franciscus de Mendoza had granted authority to investigate all the Jews throughout the three ecclesiastical electorates, and to rage against them with fire and sword) rightly said that this counsel was unjust and most wicked, and that more is accomplished through moderation and kindness than through cruelty or savagery, in his German Apology, p. 42. The same was noted by [Johannes] Pfefferkorn [d. 1523] and others. Therefore, the better and more common opinion, both among theologians and among jurists, is that the Jews should be tolerated—not indeed enticed, but, where they are found, not treated more harshly. t: Must so many efforts be used to force from us [French protestants] that French heart that God and birth has given us? What have we done to merit so many misfortunes and such severe punishments? We are hunted, we are drove up and down as if we were the plagues of the Republic; We are treated as the enemies of the Christian name. In places where the Jews are tolerated, they have all manner of liberty, they exercise arts and merchandise; they are physicians, they are consulted, the health and life of Christians is put into their hands: And as for us, as if we were infected, we are forbidden to approach children that come into the world, we are banished from the bars and faculties, we are removed from the king’s person, we are banished from societies, our charges are taken from us, we are forbidden the use of all means that might secure us from being famished; we are abandoned to the hatred of the people, we are deprived of that precious liberty that we had purchased by so many services; our children are taken from us, who are a part of ourselves; we are made to lead a languishing life, in lowness, in poverty, and often in dark prisons. Formerly, when declarations were made against us, they were at most contented with registering them in the rolls. They are at present fixed up, they are cried about the streets as if they were gazettes, to inspire the people with a spirit of fury against us. And they have been so successful that in the great cities of France we expect to have our throats cut, one time or another, by a popular sedition; so that we are very near the Inquisition. Can it be said that there is liberty of conscience in a kingdom where the people are banished, lose their honor, and their goods are confiscated for religion’s sake? There needs nothing more than fire; and that terrible tribunal of the Inquisition, which France has been hitherto so much afraid of, will be established there. Are we Turks, are we infidels? We believe in Jesus Christ, we believe him the eternal Son of God, we invoke him solely; and we have no idols. We have a sovereign respect for the sacred Scriptures, we believe there is a Heaven and a Hell, the maxims of our morality are of so great a purity, that they dare not contradict them. We have a respect for kings, we are good subjects, good citizens, faithful in commerce: Let us be tried according to law, and it will appear if we have been engaged in any conspiracy against the State, and if we have any ways failed in our duty. Thanks be to God, nothing can stagger our fidelity, and the stock of love we have for our prince is not to be drained: if it depended on our enemies, we should be enemies of the State we make a part of; they design to push us on to crimes, that the king may have a just occasion of ruining us; but they have hitherto missed their aim, and are like to do so still; the king may see it, whilst that they so successfully turn the effects of his goodness from us, there is not one of us but who is ready to lose his life for his sake; we are Frenchmen as well as we are Reformed Christians; we would shed to the very last drop of the blood of our veins to serve our king, and for the preserving our religion, even to death.

When a deliberation is instituted concerning the Jews, two extremes in particular must be studiously avoided: The one is rash expulsion; the other is licentious toleration. Jews are to be held as the servants of servants, and therefore they are to be treated harshly and compelled to perform services, to chop wood, to carry away dung and to perform other rustic labors. For they were sent by God into exile and delivered into servitude on account of the crucifixion of his Son and the contempt of the Gospel. Therefore, so that they may know that they are slaves, and may not boast on account of the prerogative of their seed, nor be emboldened in their blasphemies, the harshest burdens must be imposed upon them, nor should it be permitted that they remain idle and live exempt from labors. Hence Luther, vol. 8 (Jena). In his Book on the Jews, he gave this counsel:

t: Question 9, Whether Jews in a Christian magistracy are to be tolerated, and how are they to be dealt with? There are extreme opinions concerning this question. The first sentence is of those who absolutely deny that Jews ought to be at all tolerated in a Christian commonwealth. The moments of their assertion they advance are these: (1) Jews are extremely blasphemous; for at the name of Jesus, if they alone be present, thy cry out and say: “Let his name be blotted out”; they call the Holy Trinity nonsense and foolishness, they call Christ a spurious one; they call Mary, the blessed mother of the Savior, dung; they curse every Christian magistrate, they reckon Christians among the most lost and damned men; they think it lawful to despoil and kill Christians and treat Christian rites as obscene. (2) They think Christians to be plainly objects of hatred and enemies to God; they bring accusations against secular and principal Christian commonwealths and so separate themselves. The second judgment, plainly contrary to the first, proposes causes of hope and arguments and proofs of foundations: (3) From those things themselves is Christ made according to the flesh, Rom. 9:2, 5. A corrupt religion is extremely blasphemous: to be possessed of the habitation of the Jews within the commonwealth yields very many benefits to Christians: for they show spectacles and thereby furnish a divine mirror against the contemners of the Gospel, and they can serve for the restoration of the integrity of the monuments of the Old Testament, and confirm the truth among the images of divine predictions, Rom. 1:22. They enrich the commonwealth with money, with trade, they make it opulent and wealthy. (4) The ejection of the Jews out of the republic would carry with it many inconveniences: for being utterly expelled from Christian dominions they are more difficult to be converted and more free to blaspheme, and the Turkish kingdom would be augmented by their resources. (5) It is necessary therefore that Jews live somewhere, if any political use proper to them be by them entirely prescribed: wherefore it is preferable that they live under a Christian magistracy, as under which the hope of a more abundant conversion would shine forth than that living under a gentile magistracy they either persevere in their idolatry or pass over to the blasphemy of the gentiles. The third opinion is intermediate, since it concedes indeed that Jews may be tolerated in a Christian republic, but under certain cautions and conditions. In these conditions to be prescribed, the sentiment is not the same of the Pontiffs and the Lutheran doctors. Becanus the Jesuit, in the Manual of Controversies, bk. 3, ch. 18, pp. 728–29, 1–3, etc., embraces by three conclusions the opinion of the Pontiffs. The summary of the dissertation is that the magistrate can permit the vices and exercises of the Jews if there be a sufficient cause; that the magistrate can also permit usages of theirs, if sufficient cause be known; that the Christian magistrate cannot in good conscience permit, nor leave unpunished the external hatred of the Jews toward Christians. The Lutherans, however, concede to Jews dwelling in a Christian republic under other cautions and conditions, namely: 1. That a free exercise of religion be not conceded to them: circumcision is forbidden to them: polygamy is not permitted. 2. Blasphemy is to be punished in them very severely and restrained by most grave punishments. 3. No public office is to be entrusted to them. 4. That that monstrous usury, by which they drive Christians out, be not permitted. 5. That they be compelled to attend Christian sacred assemblies. 6. That care be taken lest they lead Christians away to the Jewish religion. Which and similar conditions and cautions about tolerating Jews in a Christian republic are required by: D. Helvicus in his System of Judaical Controversies, list of Jews 8, or the last; D. Hutterus in L.C., article 32.9.6, p. 1,037. Dn. D. Gerhardus, tome. 6, thesis 223 of Common Places, article on the Political Magistrate, pp. 890–91 ff., and the theologians of the Jena Academy in their counsel on this matter in the year 1611, and the Theological Faculty of the Academy of Frankfurt on the Oder in the year 1613, reported by Dedekennus, vol. 2, pt. 2, p. 139 ff. & 146 ff. Those conditions were conceived and prescribed piously and prudently, yet they are such that they are more easily desired than obtained. For who indeed could obtain this from the Jews, that they refrain from blasphemies against Christ and from unjust and biting usuries? For if they do not blaspheme Christ openly, yet privately they do not cease to be vexatious with shameful dealings. And he takes away a Jew’s life who prohibits usury to him; for he cannot do without it any more than he can do without common air. But how grave a sin it is to draw the yoke with unbelievers, or to grant them hospitality and the right of citizenship, since they hold a doctrine different from the doctrine of Christ, is more evident from the Scriptures than to require proof. Therefore Luther also, in Disput. Fratr., 8, in Epist., fol. 94 ff., judges with more deliberation concerning the Jews.

t: Question 8, Is it lawful to tolerate the synagogues of the Jews, in which they blaspheme the name of Jesus? Although there is no lack of rescripts of civil and canon law by which synagogues are permitted to the Jews, and it is granted that they should neither be killed, nor violated, nor hindered in their festivals (L. nullus, et L. die, Sabbathi, C. de Judæis, l.6; C. de paganis; see also the sanction of Theodoric, King of the Romans, in Goldast. Regis, apud Goldast., vol. 3 and of Emperor Conrad IV, vol. 2, Constit. Emper.) Yet it cannot be permitted with a safe conscience that they freely blaspheme the Lord Jesus in their synagogues and curse Him, or that they seduce Christians, nor are marriages to be entered into with them unless the hope of conversion to the Christian faith shines forth, nor are negotiations or autonomy to be granted to them on Sundays and other Christian festivals, but rather they are to be treated as exiles and servants and marked with a certain sign of a harmful sect: Ἀναγκἀνῷ [sp.? “Compel”]. Liberty is to be permitted to those passing over to the Christians, and the way opened to them, with laws established for hearing evangelical sermons, and for attending instruction from the writings of the New Testament by those who are exceptionally skilled in the Hebrew language and the original text. Nor do those rescripts abolish such laws, provided that coercion of faith, which is hostile to conscience, is absent, since Lk. 14:23, ἀναγκασοὺς [compel] is prescribed for the ministry, not as civilly coercive, but morally persuasive. Let there be , however, a sincere intention of leading miserable men to the faith of Christ, and let those means by which we might win them over be piously employed, such as friendly admonitions and gentle persuasions (with harshness removed), and above all clear arguments and illustrious proofs from Scripture that conquer the mind: which God blesses, as the examples of many thousands converted to the Christian Faith from the 5th to the 15th century testify. See Jerome of the Holy Faith, Book Against the Jews, and the preface of the same; Beda, qv. 30, on 1 Kings; Council. Toletan. ch. 57 etc. Although indeed by the right of political superiority no one can be forced to the Faith, as Thomas teaches, pt. 2 of 2, q. 10, art. 8, yet that Jews cannot be compelled to hear the faith is Ἀναγκάζον [constraining], because this is purely extrinsic, and a παιδαγωγός [guide]: but that [faith] embraces an intrinsic act tending toward the intellect itself and the will.

t: Concerning the first, thus: it seems that they are not to be tolerated: 1. For they blaspheme both against Christ and against the blessed Virgin; they also persecute the catholic Faith, and they inflict injury upon the ecclesiastical sacraments, as is had in the Extravagants, On the Jews, Etsi Iudaeos. But blasphemers, according to the Old Law also, were to be handed over to death; therefore the Jews too are not to be tolerated, but to be exposed to death, especially those who conduct themselves thus. 2. Furthermore, in their book, which is called the Talmud, many things were contained that pertained to the blasphemy of Christ and the blessed Virgin; since therefore they observe the doctrine of that book as though it were a law, together with books of this sort they must be destroyed. 3. Likewise, Christians persecute pagans even to death, who are the holders of the Holy Land; but an insult to the Redeemer is a greater injury; therefore Christians ought to persecute those who perpetrate such an insult even to death; therefore they are not to be tolerated. But that they inflict an insult is evident from what is said in the Extravagants, On the Jews, In nonnullis. On the contrary: a. By what is said in the Psalm, on that verse: ‘Kill them not,’ the Gloss says: ‘This can be taken especially of the Jews;’ he prays that the Jews may not perish utterly: for they have indeed been dispersed in order that they may be provoked to conversion; and he also said concerning them: ‘Kill not those who killed me, but let the nation of the Jews remain with the sign of circumcision.’ They are to be tolerated. b. Likewise, testimony that is received from adversaries is stronger; but the catholic Church takes testimony from the Old Law, which the Jews observe; therefore, in order that the catholic Church may have testimony from enemies, the Jews are to be tolerated: for from the Old Law, namely from the Law of Moses and the Prophets, testimony about Christ is taken, which they cannot deny. c. Likewise, Isa. 10:22 has that the remnant of Israel shall be saved; and similarly the apostle says, Rom. 11:5; but the remnant could not be saved unless the seed of the Jews remained; therefore the seed of the Jews must be saved; therefore the Jews are to be tolerated. This must be granted. [Replies to objections:] 1. To the contrary objection, however, it must be said that although they commit blasphemy, still they believe that they are not sinning in this, because they do not yet believe that the Messiah has come, and in this they err and are reserved for future damnation unless they come to their senses, as is said on that verse of the Psalm: ‘I will repay them.’ The Gloss: ‘In the present however, they should persist in manifest blasphemy, so that they may be dispersed; in the future, so that they may be condemned. They ought to be restrained by secular princes, as is had in the Extravagants, On the Jews, In nonnullis, where it is said: in the provinces we most strictly forbid that they presume to burst forth into insult against the Creator; and since we ought not to conceal the reproach of Him who has wiped away our reproaches, we command that such presumptuous persons be restrained by secular princes with the addition of worthy punishment, lest they presume in any way to blaspheme the Crucified for us. 2. To the second it must be said that their books, in which blasphemies of this sort are contained, ought to be burned; but they themselves, if they should persist pertinaciously in blasphemy of this sort and are convicted before a judge, are to be punished with a fitting penalty. But it is otherwise if they blaspheme secretly. 3. To the third it must be said that there is a different reason concerning the pagan holders of the Holy Land themselves and concerning the Jews themselves. For Christians persecute those pagans as unjust holders and violators of a sacred place, to the injury of Christ; but the Jews are permitted to live and to dwell among Christians for many reasons, both because from the Jews we have received the Old Law, and because Christ came from that seed, then because the promise of their salvation was made; when the fullness of the gentiles shall have entered into Christ, they are to be restrained by due admonition; nor does it seem that greater pardon should be shown to them in manifest offenses than to evil Christians.

t: Second, it is asked whether their rites are as it were idolatry. That it seems so: 1. From the fact that it is said in Gal. 5:1, on the words, “Do not again be entangled with the yoke of bondage,” the Gloss says: “This bondage is not lighter than that of idolatry,” because the servitude of the legal observances is likened to idolatry in burden. 2. And again, it is said on the words in Gal. 4:9: “To whom do you wish to serve again?” the Gloss says: “The observance of the Law.” From this it is had that the servitude of the Law, to which they were then devoted, was a sin nearly equal to the servitude of idols, to which before their conversion they had been given over, and is as it were idolatry. And this is explained there by what follows: “The Law after Christ does not differ greatly from ancient idolatry”; it is manifestly shown that the servitude of the Law is now as it were idolatry. On the contrary. a. The Law prescribed believing in God and rendering to Him alone latria [worship]; but idolatry requires the contrary: for it rendered latria to the idols themselves; therefore the servitude of the Law is in no way equal to idolatry in sin. [Solution]: 1-2. To this it must be said that it is not an equal sin for the Jews themselves to observe the rite of the legal observances and to commit idolatry; but it is said to be a sin for those themselves who have assumed the Christian Faith, nearly equal because in both cases there is apostasy, though not equal. As to burden also it had likeness: for in both cases the burden was greatest, and therefore the sacrifices of the Jews were rejected just as those of the gentiles were. But it is said not to differ from idolatry because in both cases there was unbelief. For the Galatians, when they were gentiles, served the superstition of idolatry; but when they drew back from the catholic Faith, which forbade it, they again fell into the servitude of the legal observances, as it were into unbelief. Furthermore, by reason of the performed act, namely sacrifices, there was agreement with idolatry; also by reason of the propensity to sacrifice and of the superstition itself in sacrifices. Yet for the Jews it is not so great a sin now to adhere to the Law as was the sin of those who adhered to idols.

t: Fourth, it is asked whether they are to be compelled to the Faith by threats and certain penalties. That they are not, it seems: a. For it is said in the Council of Toledo: “The holy synod has ordered concerning the Jews.” And this same thing Gregory says: henceforth to force no one into believing. For just as a man, obeying the serpent by his own will of choice, perished, so, when the grace of God calls him, each one is saved by believing through the conversion of his own mind. Therefore they are not to be driven by force, but rather to be given themselves. Gregory. It remains, therefore, that they are not to be compelled to the faith. b. Likewise, Augustine says: “We can do something unwillingly, yet we cannot believe unless of our own will one is to be led to the faith.

t: On occasion of this question it is asked whether those who come to the Faith from the Jews are to be received quickly or not, and similarly it can be asked concerning pagans. And it seems that not: a. from the fact that it is said in dist. 4, On Consecration, Jews, where it is said that for eight months they should enter within the catechumens of the church this threshold, and, if they are known to come with pure faith, only then should they merit the grace of baptism; the same is found there, Lest, which God forbid, where it is said that abstinence for forty days is enjoined. In both places therefore a great space of time is given for probation and for the work of penance to be carried out. But the contrary seems true: 1. From the fact that it is said, Acts 2:38, where Peter speaks to the Jews, saying: ‘Repent, and let each one of you be baptized.’ Since therefore they were baptized quickly, by his example it does not seem that reception into the Faith, or the sacrament of Faith, which is Baptism, should be deferred so long. 2. Likewise it is found, Acts 10:47-48, where it is said by Peter: ‘Can anyone forbid water, so that those who have received the Holy Spirit should not be baptized? And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.’ Acts 8:36-38. From these things therefore it seems that so great a delay is not fitting. [Solution]: To which it must be said that things were otherwise in the primitive Church in part and otherwise in the progress of the Church. For in the primitive Church there was the gift of the Holy Spirit, which was also shown in a visible sign in believers; there were also other signs manifesting faith in them; on account of which it was not necessary to defer the sacrament of Faith. But in the progress of the Church, where there were no such signs showing or powerfully proving faith, and hypocrisy of heart was hidden or could be hidden, a delay of time was necessary, so that there might be a testing of faith and catechesis, through which there would be enabling for baptism. And therefore according to the different times a different term was appointed according to earlier and later, so that it might be clear concerning the enabling for faith and that the ease of returning to vomit might be removed in the judgment of a discerning prelate, according as more or less it shall seem expedient. But such a term is left to the judgment of a discerning prelate, according as more or less it shall seem expedient.

t: Secondly it is asked whether Jews or pagans can be over Christians or not. And it seems that yes: 1. From the fact that the apostle says, 1 Tim. 6:1: Let all who are under the yoke of slavery deem their masters worthy of all honor. Gloss: ‘Under the yoke of infidels.’ Therefore the apostle does not deny that infidels were able to be over the faithful. 2. Likewise, Extra, Of Many: Because to be cultivated. Therefore Jews can be over Christians. They have clung more longly to their lands, as owing to a contract of the place, let them remain for the cultivation of fields, rendering the customary payments to the aforesaid Christian men. 3. Likewise, they are able to receive a price for Christian slaves that have been purchased; which would not be the case unless they were able in some way to be over them, as is found in dist. 54, Fraternitatem. 4. It also seems so from what Gelasius says, XVII, question 4, where it is said that diligently. From this it seems that your care should faithfully examine the truth of affairs, so that neither religion may seem violated, nor a slave lying by this objection, strive to decline the rights of the rightful master, whom it is not certain to be a Christian, from the dominion of his master is not to be exempted. But the contrary seems true: a. From what is said in the Decretals, Multorum, where it is said: To no Jew. And it says that it is lawful to retain a Christian slave in his dominion, but, if any are found among them, let their freedom be preserved for them. Gregory: Whatever Christian slaves a Jew is found to have purchased, bring them without ambiguity to freedom according to the precepts of the laws, lest, God forbid, the Christian religion, made subject to the Jews, be polluted. b. Likewise, in dist. 54: No public offices are to be imposed on Jews by which they may be granted the punishment of inflicting upon Christians; let Christians have Jews as masters. But this was done so that to the Jews c. Likewise, it is found in the Decretals, On the Jews, where it is prohibited, To these things for all Christians. And this same thing is found there, when they expose themselves for some wage to the service of the Jews, as is continually said: Jews or Saracens, etc. But what reason is there that, on account of the Christian faith, the right over a slave should be taken away from him, since servitude was introduced by divine law and approved also by canon law? But the Christian religion does no wrong to anyone. [Solution]: To this it must be said that a Christian is not permitted to serve a Jew, on account of avoiding damage to the Christian religion, as is found in the Decretals, On the Jews, To these things for all, where it is said: The customs of the Jews and ours in no way agree. For this same reason also, if some, because of continual conversation and assiduous familiarity, are easily able to incline the minds of the simple to their superstition and faithlessness, and they themselves should be their slaves, let them be freed from their service, sometimes at a price being given, sometimes at no price being given. For a slave of a Jew is either homeborn or purchased. If homeborn, if he is or wishes to become a Christian, he is immediately snatched away into freedom, with no price given, as is found in the Code, On bishops, and dist. 54, Fraternitatem. But if he is purchased, either he was a Christian when he was bought or a pagan. If a Christian, he becomes free, with no price given; as is found in dist. 54, Mancipia, trade in Christians is forbidden to Jews, both by the law of the land and by the law of the forum. But if he was a pagan, either he was bought for the sake of service or for the sake of commerce. If for the sake of service, and he wishes to become a Christian, he becomes free without price, dist. 54, Fraternitatem. But in the second case, if within three months afterward he has not put him up for sale if he wishes to become a Christian, he is freed without price, because it is presumed that he bought him in order to serve. But if he has put him up for sale within that term and he wishes to become a Christian then or afterward, provided that the fault did not rest with the master so that he did not sell him, he is freed, the price of twelve solidi being returned by some Christian, dist. 54, Frater, and nitatem. Decretals, In the present council: If, however, a Jew shall circumcise one wishing to become a Christian, or shall imprint the mark of another sect, he is freed without price for the injury of his own body, dist. 54, Nulla, where it is said that if certain Christians have been defiled by them in Jewish rite or even circumcised, without the price being returned let them return to freedom and the Christian religion, but human law inflicts a heavier punishment. But what has been said about the slaves of the Jews can be said about the slaves of the Saracens: for the same suspicion and the same danger can exist in both. [To the objections]: 1. To the objection, however, on the contrary it must be said that that of the apostle is understood for the state of the primitive Church and so that unbelieving masters might be enticed to the conversion of faith through the services of faithful slaves. Hence the Gloss says: Rather, unbelieving masters are converted through the services of faithful slaves. But there is added there in the text: Lest the name of the Lord and doctrine be blasphemed. The Gloss: ‘As though of one invading what is another’s.’ According to that reasoning, it will seem to someone, and Christian doctrine will seem as if unjust, that it is also now so to be done. But to this it must be answered that another reason restores the pact. For now they ought not to serve, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed; for thus Jews and pagans are inclined to this, that they may draw the faithful into faithlessness or apostasy. On account of which cohabitation with Jews and pagans, unless for the sake of preaching, is forbidden, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed. Nor ought Christian doctrine on this account to seem unjust, since the caution of faith must be preferred to all. 2. To the second, however, it must be said that, although Christians may cultivate the landed estates of Jews, they ought not nevertheless to serve Jews in their house, lest bad familiarity be contracted. And from this they are not said rightly to be over them as over slaves, because they cannot transfer them to another place or to another service, as is said in the Decretals, On the Jews. And this was done in favor of Christians, not of Jews, that they may cultivate the landed estates or lands bought from Jews, because they had formerly lived in those lands. 3. To the third, however, it must be said that, although they may receive the price of servitude, nevertheless not for Christians already existing, but for pagans who wish to become Christians. For by the law of the land Christian slaves are freed from the service of Jews, lest there be danger to the Christian faith. In favor also of the Christian faith, to certain men wishing to receive Christianity freedom is granted. 4. But that which is said in XVII, question 4, does not expressly give to understand that he was a Christian, but that he said that he had been a Christian from infancy, and that the mark of circumcision had been impressed on him by the aforesaid lord, he would be freed. But if he was not a Christian, he is not to be freed from servitude by the fact that he has fled to the church, unless he wishes to become a Christian, and this canon seems to say this. Hence it is not introduced for the dominion of Jews, but for the dominion of Christians: for some wished to defraud their master of his own right, fleeing to the enclosures of the Church. 5. To the last it must be said that the catholic Church intends to do injury to no one, but has ordered this so that no injury be done to God; but injury would be done to God if faith in something were endangered on account of the observance of temporal justice.
