t: 2. Touching the second difference, which is their vocation or calling, we must note that there is a twofold calling, vel [either] 1. Inefficaciter, formally, or effectually[?]. 2. efficaciter, formally, or effectually. The 1. is outwardly: the 2. is inwardly. The 1. general: the 2. special. Of the first, our Savior says ‘Many are called, but few are chosen.’ (Mt.) Of the second, the apostle says, ‘whom He has predestinated, them He calls,’ (Rom. 8) i.e. effectually. Now touching the outward calling, we must note that as many are called, so He calls them many ways, especially: 1. By the painful preaching of his Word. 2. By the manifold benefits of his grace. 3. By the manifest judgments of his anger. De [concerning] 1. God gave his Word, and great were the number of the preachers (God calls us diverse ways. Ps. 68:11), and He commanded them to preach unto all nations; and so their sound went unto all lands, to all countries, to all places, but especially to this place, where there are painful men, learned men that do often preach and continually call; and yet I fear their preaching is unrespected, I am sure themselves are unregarded… … … 2. God seeks to draw men unto Him in the chains of love, when He gives unto them, beneficia nimis copiosa multa, et magna, et privata, et positiva, many and great blessings, thereby to allure them unto his service. 3. If men will not turn, nor answer to the first and second call, then will He whet his glittering sword and his hand shall take hold of vengeance, He will pour out the vial of his wrath, thereby to convert them or confound them: and no marvel, for debet amor laesus irasci, love too much provoked must wax angry. All these ways has God called us: the preachers cried, and do cry and call continually, his blessings have been manifold and his judgments have been manifested in some measure upon our nation. O then let us take heed unto ourselves and not harden our hearts any longer, but let us hearken unto his voice, lest He swear in his wrath that we shall not enter into his rest. But indeed all these kinds of outward callings are but in vain, and bring no benefit unless the Lord calls us inwardly by his Spirit, for: 1. Nisi spiritus adsit cordi audientis, inanis est labor docentis (‘In vain is all outward calling, unless we be inwardly called by God’s Spirit.’ Gregory, Homily 30, Super Evangel.): In vain do we preach unto your ears, unless the Spirit of God does open your hearts, as He did the heart of Lydia, that you may believe our preaching, as she did the preaching of Paul. 2. All the blessings of the world will but puff us up with pride (as they did the Israelites, as Moses shows, dilectus meus impinguatus calcitrauit, my beloved, fatted and enlarged, spurned with his heels) unless God does give us the grace to use those blessings to the glory of his name. 3. All punishments and all judgments will sooner work desperation than conversion in a sinful soul, unless the grace of God work true humility in us, to make a right use of his fatherly chastisements. And this experience daily shows: First, the Word is preached, the one believes, the other refuses it. Secondly, God bestows his blessings upon men, the one is puffed up with pride, the other is truly thankful. Thirdly, God sends his judgments, the one grows desperate with Saul, the other is humbled with David. And what is the cause of this? to the one sort, He sends his messengers only to call them outwardly, to the other sort He sends his Spirit and gives his grace to make them yield unto his calling: and this effectual calling of the saints to believe the Gospel and to obey the voice of God is the effect and fruit of the love of God. Whensoever therefore we be outwardly called by what way or means soever it be, let us presently pray to God that He would inwardly work in our hearts to incline them to yield unto his calling, else will the outward calling bring no benefit, but only make us without excuse. And so much of their vocation.

t: For the first: the calling of God is either particular or general. The particular is to serve God in some set function of outward life, and so is the 〈…〉. The general calling is to the service of 〈…〉 with promise of eternal reward through the 〈…〉 Christ. This general calling is likewise of three sorts: 1. External. 2. Internal: or both 3. external and internal. 1. The external alone is called common and ineffectual: the 2nd and 3rd is called singular and effectual. 1. The outward calling is the work of God’s grace in his Word, offering Christ and calling upon all sorts of men to reform their ways and receive Christ, and yield obedience to God’s holy will to their salvation, if they will obey. 2. The inward calling is the work of God’s Spirit, effectually stirring up and persuading the elect to hear and obey, and receive Christ unto salvation. 3. The calling that is both inward and outward is the action of God both by his Word and Spirit, calling out his elect by name particularly and persuading them to separate from the world and receive the covenant of God’s grace in Christ, and to devote themselves to holiness of life;

t: First, that it does not follow necessarily that whosoever has that taste there mentioned [in 1 Pet. 2:3] shall not be saved: for men may have that taste, and finding it ineffectual, go on till they find a true taste: That taste is dangerous if men fall away, else there may be good use of those tastes: For it brings men near the kingdom of God and makes preparation for true grace.
w: Commentary on 1 & 2 Peter

t: [19] Q. What is the outward theological calling? An. It is medium ad salitem [a means to salt], as the word and sacraments and the members of the visible church belong unto it. [20] Q. What is that inward theological calling? An. It is when God’s word brings [God’s word’s ring?] does not rest in our outward ears but comes into the heart and works somewhat there. [21] Q. How many ways [is] this taken? An. It is either effectual or ineffectual. [22] Q. What is the inward ineffectual calling? An. When it comes into the heart and falls as on stony ground. [23] Q. How far may this inward ineffectual calling bring us? An. To these four degrees of grace principally. 1. It may bring a man to see his own sin & misery. 2ly. It may so work upon him, as it may bring him to have a desire after the thing persuaded [for?] 3ly It may bring him to some kind of degree of possession of the thing called for. 4ly It may bring him to some outward correspondence, as to reform many sins. [24] Q. Why then is it called an ineffectual calling? An. Because it does not fully persuade [the] heart to come in. … [30] Q. By what wording in scripture is our vocation expressed? An. By many expressions: as first by alluring and persuading. Hos. 2:14. 2ly by inviting and compelling. Math 22:4. 3ly by stretching out of the hand. Rom. 10:21. 4ly by beseeching, 2 Cor. 5:20. 5ly by drawing us. John 6.44. Lastly by apprehending. [31] Q. Do all these properly belong to effectual calling? An. No, the four first may be applied to ineffectual calling. … [38] Q. Whither do effectual and ineffectual calling differ in this respect or no, do not both come from God? An. They agree in this that both proceed from God, yet they differ in regard of the manner of work, for God does the work not secundum propositum [according to the purpose], but secundum obviam [according to the thing encountered]. … [55] Q. What and how many are the instrumental causes of our vocation? An. They are of two sorts either primary or secondary? [56] Q. What were the primary? An. The word. [57] Q. In what propositions was that expressed? An. James 5:11 [1:21?] suggests the word is the ordinary means whereby He calls and so by consequence the ministry of it. 2d. That it was but an instrumental cause under God and so it’s called the [sassed?] of God, the arm of god and sometime the power of God. 3ly. That as it’s but an instrumental cause so it did only belong to those which are adults, for infants may be said to be sanctified but not called. 4. That it was but a separable instrument. [58] Q. How can we say if the converting word is a separable means? An. For two reasons: Because the word may be without the Spirit. 2. Because the Spirit may be and may call some without the word. … [86] Q. Now you have spoken of the primary instruments of salvation as the word and sacraments. What are the secondary instruments? An. They are many as: 1. The mercies and favors of God common to all. Rom. 10:21 [“But to Israel he saith, All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people.”]. Bounty is one thing that may cause love so that one main instrument or means God uses to call us home which is to draw us with the thick cords of love [Hos. 11:4]. … [95] Q. Whether do effectual and ineffectual calling differ in this [Q: 94: ‘who are they whom God is thus pleased to call’]? An. Yes, for the ineffectual calling, many are called but few are chosen.
w: A Brief & Pithy Catechism

t: Doctrine 3. All those, and those alone, make their election sure that make their calling sure. These two God has joined together, as the apostle does in this place, so that no man ought or may disjoin them. Hence election and calling are taken sometimes in the Scriptures for one and the same, as 1 Cor. 1:26-27, that which is called ‘calling,’ verse 26, is called ‘election,’ verse 27. There is indeed an outward and ineffectual calling, which is many times separated from election, as when it is said, ‘Many are called, but few are chosen.’ But effectual and saving calling has always a sure connection with election, Rom. 8:3•[30?] and 11:28-29.
w: An Analytical Exposition of both the Epistles of the Apostle Peter

t: We have spoken at large of the participation of the grace of Christ and the benefits of the Gospel: Now we are come unto the means whereby God does effect these things. Show therefore how and in what manner God does offer and communicate the Covenant of Grace unto mankind? By vocation or calling, Rom. 8:30; Heb. 3:1, when God, by the means of his Word and Spirit acquainting men with his gracious purpose of salvation by Christ, invites them to come unto Him, Hos. 2:14, and revealing unto them his Covenant of grace, Mt. 11:27; 16:17; Jn. 14:21; Ps. 25:14, brings them out of darkness to light, Acts 26:18. Is this calling of one sort only? No: there is an external gathering common to all, together with some light of the Spirit and certain fruits of the same, attained unto by some that are not heirs of the promise: for many are called with this outward and ineffectual calling, who are not chosen, Isa. 48:12; Mt. 22:14. And there is an internal and effectual calling, peculiar to those few that are elect; whereby unfeigned faith and true repentance is wrought in the heart of God’s chosen; and God (become in Christ their Father) does not only outwardly by his Word invite, but inwardly also, and powerfully by his Spirit allure and win their hearts to cleave to Him inseparably unto salvation, Gen. 9:27; Ps. 25:14; 60:6. 5. 4; Joel 2:32; Acts 2:39. How do both these kinds of callings differ? Howsoever we are to judge charitably of all outwardly called, 1 Cor. 1:2, because who among them is also inwardly called, is only known to God, 2 Tim. 2:19, yet does this outward calling differ from the inward. 1. In that it is wrought only by outward means, and common illumination, Heb. 4:2, without the spirit of regeneration, Jude verse 19, or any portion of saving faith, Lk. 8:13. 2. In that they are admitted only to an outward and temporary league of formal profession, Acts 8:13; Rom. 9:4-5, not to that entire fellowship with Christ required unto salvation, 1 Jn. 2:19; 1 Cor. 1:8-9. What are the means which God has appointed to call us by? They are partly inward, and partly outward, 1 Thess. 5:19-20; Acts 10:44. What are the inward? The Spirit of God, which is given by the outward things, Gal. 3:2-3; 1 Tim. 1:14. What mean you by the Spirit of God in this place? That power of God which works in the hearts of men things which the natural discourse of reason is not able to attain unto. Being incomprehensible, how may we come to some understanding and sense of it? By the things whereunto it is compared: 1. To wind, Acts 2, to show the marvelous power of it in operation. 2. To oil, Heb. 1:9, that is of a hot nature that pierces and supplies. 3. To water, Jn. 4, that cools, scours and cleanses. 4. To fire, Mt. 3; Acts 2, that severs dross and good metal. How is the operation of it? Diverse; as softening and hardening, enlightening and darkening, which it works after a diverse manner, by the Word in the hearts of the elect and reprobate, according to the good pleasure of God’s secret will only, and after that, according to the good pleasure of his revealed will; so that the lawful use thereof is rewarded with a gracious increase of blessing, and the abuse punished with further hardness to condemnation. What then does the Spirit work in the wicked? Finding them hard, it hardens them more to their further condemnation. What does the same Spirit work in the godly? Faith, whereby they take hold on Christ with all his benefits, Eph. 2:8. What are the outward things which God has given to call us by? They are either common to the whole world, or proper to the Church. What are the things common to the whole world? God’s works not unprofitably given, although not sufficient to salvation. Is not the knowledge of the wisdom, power and goodness of God in the creation and government of the heaven and earth, with the things that are in them, sufficient to make us wise to salvation? No: First, it serves rather for further condemnation without the Word, Rom. 1:19-21. Secondly, as by and with the Word, the due meditation and consideration of God’s works is a good help to further us in religion and in the graces of God’s Spirit, 1 Cor. 1:21-22.

t: The persons called by God, who yet are not chosen, are of two sorts, as you heard: First, those, who, though so graciously invited, do yet obstinately and peremptorily refuse, and these are actively only called on God’s part. The second sort is of those who do give consent, and yield to their call, but because they do not rise up fully to all that is required, therefore they are cast away. In this [latter] rank is the man, who being invited, made no opposition or excuse, but went in and sat down at the feast, was as confident as the other guests, seems to be conscious to himself of no fault, but having no wedding garment, the master is so wroth and displeased with him, that he is adjudged to everlasting torments; and from this instance our Savior gathers this conclusion in the text [circa Mt. 22:14]; so that the meaning is: Of those many that are called , and give a general acceptance of it, yet few are chosen to eternal glory: Those enjoy the feast of the ordinances here, who are to be tormented for ever hereafter; those are admitted to eat in God’s presence here, who shall be commanded to depart from Him hereafter, He knows them not: Many are admitted into the temple that may not enter into the holiest of holies… That men did receive the truth as to some particulars and some degrees, but not wholly and thoroughly… Thou receivest Christ and his ways but in parcels, though thou hast baptism, the title of a Christian, sittest down at the ordinances, yet where is the wedding-garment! where is the conversation that does agree and belong to so holy a matter? To open this doctrine, let us consider: First, Wherein lies this outward obedience to God’s call, which yet is ineffectual; for can anything more concern you than that you should not be Christians in vain? that all thy praying and frequenting of holy duties may not be in vain? that God may not take thee from this feast, as Haman was from his in which he so much boasted, to be put into confusion and everlasting fear?
w: Spiritual Refining: or A Treatise of Grace and Assurance

t: 3. But of that spiritual calling afforded only unto some (Acts 14:17), which is, to seek happiness and blessedness in Christ. This is twofold: 1. Only external and ineffectual. 2. Internal also and effectual. 1. Only external (Ps. 147:19-20; Acts 17:30), and by the ministry of the Gospel bestowed sometimes upon cities, kingdoms, commonwealths: A calling according to means, common to the elect and reprobates: ‘Many are called, but few are chosen’ (Mt. 20:16): It’s often inefficacious, as to the saving good of the hearer. Christ would have gathered Jerusalem’s children, and they would not. (Mt. 23:37; Heb. 4:3, Audiunt multi, obaudiunt pauci.) The Word preached profited not, because not mixed with faith; God by this external calling showing what is man’s duty, and what was once his ability to perform; the impairing of which later is no exemption from the former; (Jn. 15:22, 24) and hereby rendering men inexcusable, they knowing what they should do and not doing what they know. And also by this merely outward calling men are contained in external order, abstain from sundry great and heinous sins, are profitable instruments in a commonwealth, observe civil justice, etc. which God oft rewards with temporal blessings. 2. The other sort of this spiritual vocation is internal and effectual; this bringing us into the invisible Church, as the other into the visible…

t: 2. Why this He does (say others in the second place) by offering Himself to all, offering grace and mercy, life and salvation to all upon the condition of believing. (Omnes vocat, et omnibus salutem offert. Ferus. Mt. 23) True, such an offer Christ makes unto all, all those whom He sends the Gospel to. And so He may be said to draw all men, calling, inviting them to come unto Him; so did He draw Jerusalem in the days of his flesh, ‘O Jerusalem, how often would I have gathered thee?’ And thus He draws all those that are within the pale of the Church, the sound of the Gospel. (Musculus at the location; Ferus at the location) I dare not say with some, Quantum in se est, trahit, that as much as in Him lies, He draws all men; no, I know that if Christ put forth his power, he can overpower the soul of the most obstinate and rebellious sinner, and cause Him to come in, and that willingly: Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy powers, Ps. 110:3. When Christ puts forth the arm of his power, accompanying his Word with his Spirit (for that is the day of Christ’s power) then shall his call be effectual, all that are so called shall come to Him, and that willingly. (Isa. 65:2, Pro omnibus in cruce pependit, et omnes quantum in se est, expansis ad se brachiis veluti trahit. Musculus on Mt. 28:19 & Mk. 16:15) Thus Christ does not draw all men; yet outwardly He does, offering Himself alike to all. So He did upon the cross, where his arms were extended and spread abroad, as inviting all, willing and ready to receive and embrace all that should come to Him. There behold the Son of man lift up, and drawing all men unto Him; this He does more clearly in the preaching of the Gospel, which He requires to be published to all nations, to every creature under heaven. There He makes known Himself, offers himself to all that will receive Him, inviting, persuading them to come to Him to believe on Him. Thus He draws all in respect of an outward call; that this drawing proves ineffectual to some, to many, to the most, the fault is their own in that they do not hearken to this call, they will not follow him drawing, but draw back; ‘I would have gathered you, but ye would not,’ (Mt. 23:37) says our Savior to Jerusalem. In the mean time, Christ draws them outwardly. Thus He draws all; not that he intends to save all, but that by this means He may draw forth his elect out of all, and bring them home to Himself, even as the fisherman (the similitude illustrates it well) in drawing of his net, his drag, he draws all that comes within the compass of it, not only good fish, but weeds and stones, and mud; and wherefore does He this? why, it is for the good fishes’ sake; that what is good He may save. (Mt. 13:47) Even thus is it with Christ’s dragnet, the preaching of the Gospel; The Kingdome of Heaven is like unto a net (says our Savior): It draws all that come within the reach and compass of it, Christ offering grace and mercy alike to all. But wherefore this? why, it is for the elect’s sake: that Christ may save those which are his by that means singling and drawing them out of the world and bringing them effectually home to Himself. He draws all, that He may save some; draws all outwardly by his Word, that by his Spirit accompanying his Word, He may draw his elect out of all, making that his drawing effectual to them, to all of them. Thus Christ draws all men, a truth, but not the whole truth here intended. The drawing which our Savior here speaks of, I look upon it as an inward and effectual work, a drawing and bringing of men home unto Himself, to believe on Him.

t: And here is the instrument which Christ makes use of for the drawing of his elect to Himself: the preaching, plain and simple preaching of the Gospel, seemingly a weak and unlikely instrument; thence called the foolishness of preaching (1 Cor. 1:21); Yet by this weak means does Christ effect this great work: Hereby drawing men out of darkness from under the power of Satan. Paul was sent to the gentiles (Acts 26:18) to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God: But how was he to do it? Why, by preaching of the Gospel, by bearing the name of Christ before them (Acts 9:15), hereby drawing them out of the world as fishes out of the sea; hereby drawing them out of themselves, convincing them of their insufficiency and Christs all sufficiency; and so drawing them to Himself; first as to a Savior to believe on Him, working faith in them by this means, ‘Faith comes by hearing, hearing the Word, the word of the Gospel (Rom. 10): Then as to a Lord, to be governed by Him, which is also wrought by the same instrument. (2 Cor. 12:4-5) Here is the outward means, but this often proves ineffectual. Many there are who hear the Word, and hear it powerfully dispensed, who yet are never the better for it; so says the apostle of the Jews: The Word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it, Heb. 4:2. And so ineffectual it often proves to many that sit under the sound of it: They are not thereby brought home to Christ. Even as many of the Jews saw Christ lift up, beheld Him crucified, who yet believed not on Him, nay thereby they were hardened-against Him. Even so it is now in the preaching of the Gospel: Many there are before whose eyes Christ is lift up, crucified in the Word and sacraments, who yet are not brought to believe on Him or submit unto Him. 2. To this therefore (in the second place) is joined the Spirit, the Spirit of Christ which He sends forth to accompany his Word and to make it effectual in the hearts of his elect; and by this means He draws men effectually;

t: Use 2. Yet let their carelessness make us the more careful… Let us when we look up to God that calls us, remember his greatness. Let us, when we look downward to the misery out of which He has called us, remember the depth of it. Let us when we look forward to the honor unto which He has called us, ponder upon the height of it. Let us when we look backward upon the means whereby He has called us, consider the ineffectualness of them upon others. So shall we find the total sum to be this, That the highest God has called us out of the lowest degree of misery to the greatest step of glory out of his own grace and free mercy.

t: Explanation 31. That we may the better know what effectual calling is, we are to consider of a double call, which does many times prove ineffectual, as: (1) Outward, in the preaching of the Word and the voice of the rod or any providence whatsoever, which does call men to repentance, faith and holiness; but notwithstanding all these outward calls, there are millions in the world who turn the deaf ear to God and will not return to Him by repentance, nor come to Christ by faith. (2dly) There is an inward call which is no less ineffectual than the former, and it is the Spirit’s call, as when He proceeds no further than that which divines call a common work, as: (1.) Common illumination, or some kind of floating knowledge in the head concerning the Word of God and spiritual matters; and no doubt but many men who have wicked hearts and lead bad lives may be well stored with gifts of this kind, as Judas for one. (2.) Some kind of flashy affections excited and stirred up in the soul towards good things, called foretastes of the powers of the world to come; and such was in Herod and Balaam. (3.) Some kind of faint languishing inclinations in the will to obedience, such as Herod had when he did many things. (4.) Some kind of sense of sin, both in its guilt and horror, such as Judas had; and yet notwithstanding all this inward work of the Spirit, his call may be ineffectual. And if all this may be without success, then no wonder if the Arminians’ call, that of moral suasion, or of arguments, do prove no better. But then (2dly) There is another inward call of the Spirit, which is effectual to the elect; sc. that whereby the Spirit does not only call, but enable them to come at his call, as when He does renew the mind and change the will, sanctify the heart, purify the conscience and affections, and does work a lively faith in such persons, and repentance from dead works.

t: V. The form or manner of this calling is chiefly: (1) In the tender or offering of Christ and of all saving happiness in Him unto Sinners. (2) In sinners’ accepting, embracing or closing with this tender. 1. Christ, and all saving happiness in him, is offered or tendered unto sinners on God’s part, etc. Acts 4:12; Heb. 7:25; 1 Cor. 1:23-24; 2 Cor. 5:19-21; Mt. 22:2 to 15; Mt. 11:28-30. This tender or offer of Christ to sinners is twofold, viz. ineffectual and effectual. (1) Ineffectual, which becomes not fully efficacious to conversion and salvation. And this again is either, outward only, when Christ and his benefits are only outwardly tendered in his Gospel, New Covenant promises, etc. preached and propounded, Acts 2:38-39 & 9:15 & 13:38-39. As when the preaching of the Gospel is tendered to them that refuse to hear it, but put it from them, stop their ears against it, contradict, etc. Acts 7:57 & 13:45-46, or if they do hear it, yet do not understand it (much less assent to it) as the hearer compared to the ground by the wayside, Mt. 13:4, 19. Inward also, when the Word is not only offered and propounded to the outward ear, but also to the inward heart: So that they not only hear it, but understand it, Mt. 21:45-46. Yea sometimes not only understand it, but also by a temporary faith for a time assent to it and receive it with joy, Mt. 13:5-6, 20-21; Lk. 8:6, 13. All these degrees of calling, outward and inward, are ineffectual and insufficient to salvation: yet are they of great use, consequence and advantage to the interessing of persons in the visible Church, to the partaking of all the ordinances and means of grace, whereby much sin may be prevented and perhaps true grace may be conveyed. (2) Effectual, when Christ and his benefits are so tendered to the mind and heart in the New Covenant-doctrine that the mind is savingly illuminated to understand and the heart effectually opened to assent to the tender, and fiducially to apply it, Lk. 8:15; Eph. 1:17; Jn. 6:45; Acts 16:14 & 8:35-37. From this different tender of Christ ineffectual and effectual, arises that distinction of ineffectual calling; ‘Many are called and few chosen:’ (Mt. 22:14 & 20:26) and effectual calling, viz. according to God’s purpose of election (Rom. 8:28, 30). That may befall hypocrites and reprobates; this is peculiar only to the elect. Thus Christ and all saving happiness in Him is propounded and tendered to sinners.

t: …there remains a necessary distinction to be attended unto of God’s call, that it is twofold: either external only, or external and internal also; or an effectual and ineffectual calling. For though this distinction be hated by some men, yet the Scripture is very clear that there are many called, who yet are not chosen: and when he says called, it is not meant only actively on God’s part, as some were called, but yet refused and would not so much as outwardly profess obedience, but ‘called’ is to be understood passively on man’s part, so that he gives some outward conformity to Gods call. There is an external reception and submission to it, but yet there is no true inward sanctification: Insomuch that some who are called the children of the Kingdom shall be cast forth; and they are said not to be all Israel who are of Israel. In the Old Testament we read of many who outwardly submitted to the profession of God’s commands, who yet were not found at heart; and therefore our Savior in the course of his ministry did not direct his preaching more to any subject almost than this, viz. to have the internals of grace as well as externals; so that we may say, There is a called and elected Church, and a called Church only, not elected; and this is to take off all Churches from idolizing and doting upon the ordinances and external administrations which are in a Church, as the Jews did, and as most Christians do. We are to go further and to see whether we be indeed and really Christ’s body, as well as seemingly.

t: Fifthly, if thou art a holy person, if thou art one that hast that real holiness without which there is no happiness, then know for thy comfort, that thy holiness is a glorious witness and evidence of thy effectual vocation, 1 Pet. 1:15, ‘As He who hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation.’ Many are externally called that are not internally called, and many are ineffectually called that are not effectually called. But now real holiness that speaks out an internal call, an effectual call, a call out of darkness into marvelous light… The Author of this call is a holy God; our holy calling depends upon the purpose of God, the power of God, and the grace and good pleasure of God; the means of our holy calling are the Spirit of God and the Word of God; and the ends of our calling are holiness and the glory of God.

t: 2. God’s gracious invitation of lost sinners to Christ, which properly is his calling them, is either external or internal; external by the word, internal by his Spirit. [1.] External, by the commands and promises of the word, requiring such duties from them, and assuring them of such blessings upon obedience. Thus Wisdom’s maidens are sent forth to invite guests to her palace, Prov. 4:2; and the king’s servants to call them to the marriage-feast, Matt 22:9; and so far they prevail in their message, that many present themselves. God would not leave us to a book, but has appointed a living ministry, 2 Cor. 6:10. [2.] Internal, not only by the word, but by his Spirit, and the checks of their own conscience, which is a nearer approach of his grace and power to us. By the motions of his Spirit; how else could it be said, Gen. 6:3, ‘My Spirit shall not always strive with man’? and Acts 7:51, ‘Ye do always resist the Holy Ghost’? And also by their consciences soliciting them to the performance of their duty, and challenging them for the neglect of it. It is natural duty: Rom. 2:14,15, ‘The Gentiles do by nature the things contained in the law; these, having not the law, are a law to themselves, which show the works of the law written in their hearts; their consciences also bearing witness, and their thoughts in the meanwhile accusing or excusing one another.’ And for acceptance of the gospel-covenant: 1 John 3:20,21, ‘If our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart and knows all things; if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence towards God.’ 3. This external and internal calling may be ineffectual or effectual. [1.] The ineffectual call consists in the bare tender and offer of grace, but it is not entertained. God may knock at the door of the heart that does not open to Him; knock by the word, knock by the motions of the Spirit and checks of conscience; so ‘many are called, but few are chosen,’ Matt 22:14. There is not the fruit of election, nor are these the called according to purpose. [2.] The effectual call is when God changes the heart, and brings it home to Himself by Jesus Christ…

t: Doctrine 3. ‘Counsel of his will’. That is which his will propounded to it, [it] did freely accept. Observe hence that what God wills once, that He effectually works, see Ps. 115, ‘Our God is in heaven and does whatsoever He wills: Who has refused his will?’ so Isa. 46:10. We see in beasts that they have an appetite to that [which] they move after; in men that which they will, that they put out their power to effect; so it is in God: if He will anything, He does work it effectually. That is a frivolous distinction of an effectual and an ineffectual will in God, which stands neither with truth of Scripture, as in this place, nor with the blessedness of God, nor with the nature of things: all that showed Him, which his will accepts, He does effectually work it. [It is] Against [the] blessedness of God: for might God will a thing and not have it, He were not fully blessed, when to have every good will is more blessed than to want [lack] it. Against [the] nature of things, for everything which will and ability works, if God almighty have will to anything, the thing must needs follow. Where there is full power to work anything, applied to the working of it, the thing wrought must needs follow. Here some distinguish and say that in things which God will do, his power does work them effectually, but the things which God would have on condition from us, those his power does not work: an old Pelagian conceit. Would not God have us walk in his commandments, and has He not said that He will put his Spirit in us and make us walk in them? St. Augustine learned that God did promise to work mightily those things He requires from us. If to have the conditional will be more happy than to want it, then God who has power to work the condition in us will not want it: Not to say that this conditional will is absurdly imagined in God: He must will the having a thing on condition which He will not work, and then it is impossible, unless the creature can do something good which He will not do in him; or on condition which He will work, and then He works all He wills; or on such a condition which He sees the creature cannot perform, nor Himself will not make Him perform; and this were idle and frivolous.

t: Question: Seeing God purposed to destroy them, and did it not, is not his will alterable and inefficacious? Answer: The counsels, purposes, decrees of God are unalterable and do take place, Ps. 33:11; Isa. 14:27; 43:13; 46:10; Mal. 3:6; Heb. 6:17. For that said and done here, it’s more humano [by a human custom]: God saw cause-sufficient to move Him to their destruction, but seeing what evil was like to come about, He would not destroy them; had the Lord decreed it before the world, it must have taken place, no change or alteration could have been.

t: Thus then the morality of our actions must not be measured by any decree concerning the futurition of events, but by some other rule, in which must concur God’s will and appointment, setting bounds unto us and designing our duty, and discovering what is well-pleasing and acceptable to God, honest and laudable in itself, and profitable and comfortable to us in the issue; and thus we have the Word of God for our direction and have his laws and testimonies to be our rule: Dt. 29:29; Isa. 8:20; Dt. 30:10-12; Dt. 5:29; Ps. 147:19; Rom, 12:2; 1 Thess. 4:2; 1 Pet. 4:2, etc. and we may take notice of these three things as necessarily requisite and concurring in that which is a warrant unto and rule of our actions and petitions: 1. The good-pleasure and decree of God, not concerning what shall come to pass, but concerning the quality and moral goodness of human actions, and which does limit and set bounds to reasonable creatures and prescribes unto them their duty; and this is the fountain and first spring (yea and by many judicious and sober divines is judged to be the supreme adequate and first rule) of moral rectitude. Hence we may conceive that God’s laws in Scripture are called ‘decrees,’ ‘statutes’ and ‘ordinances’. 2. From this decree and appointment, does (to our apprehension) flow divine approbation, complacency and delight in what is thus appointed to be our work and duty: hence that appointment is called the good, acceptable and perfect will of God, Rom. 12:2, and our actions when conform[ed] to that rule, are said to be well-pleasing in his sight, Heb. 13:2; yea the Lord does not only declare his love of his complacency, and delight in these when they are performed, but also He is said to will and desire (though not according to the Jesuitical and Arminian gloss)¹ those works while He is speaking to the rebellious and disobedient who have slighted his laws and casten all his statutes behind their backs: Eze. 18:23, 32; 33:11; Hos. 6:6; 1 Sam. 15:22; Isa. 61:8; Mt. 9:13; 2 Pet. 3:9, etc. ¹ Arminians, Socinians and Jesuits from thence would collect a frustratable and inefficacious will and desire in God, but this phrase does only import God’s serious approbation of the works of righteousness and detestation of the contrary. 3. There must be an intimation and promulgation of this decree and appointment, and a declaration of those things that would be well pleasing, and acceptable to God.

t: But many testimonies of Scripture (you will say) teach that even the reprobate have known the truth. Leaving aside the Scriptures of the Old Testament: to Romans the apostle concerning the reprobates says that they hold the truth of God in unrighteousness. And to the Hebrews [6:4-6] he says that some have fallen away from the truth. And he says they taste the word of God and the powers of the world to come: but after the knowledge of the truth they willfully sin. And this is sin against the Holy Spirit: namely the opposition to the truth known, made from the heart. There are twofold cognitions of the truth (as was shown at the outset): one indeed is given and conferred by the gift of the Spirit; but yet inefficacious. For it is only on the surface of the intellect, and the ray has no root in the heart; and therefore it cannot be durable. For it is like seed which is born among rocky chinks and has no root; therefore when the sun arises it withers. Such cognition is common also to the reprobate. … Another is efficacious by the Holy Spirit, the Spirit, I say, of regeneration. For this penetrates into the heart, receives it, reforms and refashions it: there it puts down deep roots, and thrusts itself forth outward in its fruits by charity… Wherefore the Thesis remains firm: only the elect can come to the true knowledge of the truth, and at last the thing itself attains them. Thus it happens that this cognition of the truth is purely the work of the Holy Spirit, efficaciously calling and teaching. What things are demanded of us that we may come to a true and efficacious cognition of the truth? Thesis: That we be led to the cognition of the truth, besides a certain general hearing of the Word of God, we must pray that God may grant us his Spirit: who, when He excites in us the desire to seek that truth, then leads us to seek, to find, and to retain it.

t: This question is not proposed without cause by us: for on the one hand, if God’s simplicity and immutability are regarded, it will not seem in any way admissible in God that wills be contrary to one another; which also will always be done according to that saying: ‘My will shall be done: and whatsoever He hath willed He hath done.’ Yet if many passages which are handed down in Scripture be considered, we should confess: there is no one who would not say that the will of God is not one only but in a manner manifold: and very often contrary. For He commands many things which do not happen either because He cannot effect them to be, or because He does not will them to be. The former cannot be said without denying God’s omnipotence, and thus deity. Some distinguish between an antecedent will and a consequent will: as [John] Damascus, bk. 2, ch. 46. Others between the will of good-pleasure and the will of sign: as Lombard and the scholastics: Sentences, bk. 1, dist. 45. Others between a will not revealed and a will revealed. Others between absolute volition and conditional volition. Others what God wills to be done respecting us, and into the will which He wills to be from us. Some distinguish in the will of the Almighty a will efficacious and an inefficacious will, as Augustine in the Enchiridion, chs. 102-3. These divisions seem various, but if they be weighed diligently and rightly understood, they reduce to the same. … Efficacious & Inefficacious Will Thirdly, that former and absolute will is also called by Augustine, just as it is most certain, so also most omnipotent, efficacious and invincible: and this is because it is always fulfilled, as much in heaven as on earth. But the other, namely the conditional, is called by the same Augustine the inefficacious will: because, clearly, it is not always fulfilled. For since it depends on conditions which God demands of us, and we do not perform them, it happens that it is not always nor in all things fulfilled, and therefore it is deservedly called inefficacious, namely by itself alone. Let Augustine be read in volume 3, in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chs. 102-3. Some things also in volume 5, On the City of God, bk. 22, chs. 1-2. … IV. From those things which I have said, it appears, first, why, although there is only one will of God—that is, one decree concerning all things, as has been demonstrated, and that immutable—it is nevertheless said to be manifold: namely, both on account of the diverse kinds of things which God wills, and on account of the diverse manner of willing, as it seems to us: because, namely, he wills some things simply and absolutely, while other things seem to us to be willed conditionally. Then it is also clear that, although there seem to be many partitions of the divine will, all are nevertheless reduced to one partition: namely, to the absolute and secret will, which is also called the will of Good Pleasure; and to the revealed and conditional will, which is not undeservedly named the will of the sign. And thus, in the third place, it appears that, although in reality there is only one will in God, as has been declared and confirmed, it can nevertheless be said to be manifold by different respects. And conversely, although on account of the diverse reasons by which he seems to will, and by which he explains his will, many wills of his are said to exist: it does not therefore hinder that there is in reality only one will of God, and that constant and eternal: which is the head of this our thesis. For although He wills many things, and indeed willed some things, for example, in the Old Testament, but wills other things in the New: yet He willed both those and these by the same will and decree. He willed those at one time, namely, until the time of correction, as the Apostle says: he wills these at another time, until the end of the world. Behold how the diverse kinds of things which he wills do not in the least cause there to be in reality many wills of God: but one and the same will always remains in God. And although he seems to will many things absolutely, but others conditionally: in reality, however, if one must speak properly, all things whatsoever God wills, He wills absolutely and simply. And consequently, all things which He wills also come to pass. For the fact that he is said to will certain things conditionally: this is to be referred only to the manifestation of that will. For there is no conditional will in God, because this fights against his eternal wisdom: but only in the law. And this also, that He signifies in the law that He wills conditionally: He had decreed by his absolute will to do—namely, not to manifest his will concerning the saving or damning of men without a condition; and this because this would be both useful to us and would conduce to the manifesting of his justice. For it was and is useful to us the elect to know that God does not will that anyone be saved without living faith in Christ: and consequently, if we wish to be saved, that we must believe in Christ. Likewise, this conduced to rendering the reprobate inexcusable. For they know what things are necessary for salvation: and consequently, it served to vindicate the justice of God from all accusations and calumnies. Therefore, because it was expedient, He revealed his will with a condition. And in this respect, the will of God seems to be twofold: which, however, is in reality only one, and that firm and constant. For by one and constant will he absolutely wills only the elect to be saved: and consequently He wills only also by true faith, which can be kept, are given: but the reprobate, are absolutely excluded from this salvation: and therefore, are not given the faith by which they can be blessed in heaven. See how the different modes, by which God seems to will, do not remove the fact that there remains but one, eternal and absolute and immutable will of God, on account of which different modes, different wills also seem to exist. V. But that He also commands many things to be done, which are not done: it does not follow from this, however, either that He is impotent: as if He could not cause that what He commands, be done: or that there is truly a manifold will in God: one, which He signifies by word, another, which He does not will to be done in His presence, that which He commands. For there are two kinds of God’s commandments: some are simply absolute: and without any condition at all, either expressed or tacit. These are the most certain, absolute and simple testimonies of the divine will, which is called good pleasure. Such was that to Moses, do all things according to the pattern which you saw on the mountain. Likewise, Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: go into Egypt: and other commands of that kind made both to Moses himself and to the prophets. Because these are the very will of God: therefore He who gives these commands, also brings it about that they are done. And of these is that in Isaiah 46, ‘My counsel shall stand: and my will shall be done;’ and Pm. 115, ‘Whatsoever He willed, He did.’ Therefore, as far as this kind of God’s commandments is concerned: it appears that there is one and the same will: that, namely, which is revealed in the Word: and that, which was hidden in the secret counsel of God. Whence does this appear? From the fact that what God commands happens. There are other commandments, which He promulgated with a condition, if not expressed, at least tacit: such as those which we have in the law. Namely, if we wish to enter into life: that this and that is commanded to us, and that these commandments are to be kept, as Christ explained, saying: If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. All these things indeed, are proposed conditionally both to the elect and to the reprobate: meanwhile, however, these commandments have a far different reason, insofar as they are made to the elect: and another, insofar as they are made to the reprobate. Insofar as they are made to the elect: although they are proposed with a condition: yet the will of God in them is absolute. For God simply wills: that they be kept by the elect, if not always, at least at length sometime. And for this reason, because they cannot perform these things by their own strength: He gives them the strength of the Spirit, by which they can; just as He promises through Ezekiel: I will cause that you walk in my commandments. And because even with the strength which the Lord supplies, they cannot perfectly keep the commandments in themselves: He brings it about that they keep them perfectly in Christ: insofar as namely: And through Christ their transgressions are not imputed to them: and on account of Christ, their begun obedience, serving as most perfect, is accepted: and on the contrary, Christ’s justice and obedience are imputed to them: and because finally, at the end in heaven most perfectly, even in themselves, they will complete the sum of the law. In this way also it appears, that the will of God, which is revealed in the commandments: is one and the same in reality with the secret will and will of good pleasure. Therefore, neither here are there two different wills, but one. God acts in giving the law to the elect, as a parent in prescribing laws to his children. He not only teaches what He requires of them: but also signifies that He altogether wills that they keep them, whether they want to or not. But towards the reprobate, He acts as a Lord towards his servants. He will promulgate merely conditional laws: if they want to be with Him, [He wills] altogether that they conduct themselves thus: if not, let them depart. Thus God. Therefore, insofar as these commandments are given to the reprobate, and likewise promises are added to them: all are truly conditional. For the will of God is not absolute, that the reprobate keep them: or attain the promises. This is clear, both from the one example of ‘Pharaoh, I will harden, lest he let the people go:’ and from the fact that they do not keep them, neither in themselves, nor in Christ: in whom they are not: nor ever will keep them. But those things which God properly wills: He brings it about that all of them be accomplished: according to that, All things, whatsoever He willed, He did: And that in Isa. 46, ‘My counsel shall stand, and my will shall be done.’ Wherefore there is not here a double will of God in reality: one in the law, another in the mind and essence of God: for it is not the will of God that the impious should keep the law, as has been said. No one, therefore, will be able to infer in any way from the precepts of God that there is a double will in reality. I will speak more briefly and clearly. The Law can be considered in two ways: either insofar as it is Torah (doctrine), by which it is taught what is pleasing to God, and what must be done by us, or not done, if we wish to be saved: in this way the Law is taught as pertaining to all, both the reprobate and the elect. And because it reveals and teaches what is right and pleasing to God: that is therefore said to be the will of God, because it reflects the nature of God, and what God loves and approves. Or it is considered insofar as it is Torah (commandment): that is, the true testimony of the secret will, or what He wills to be done by us at all. In this way it pertains only to the elect. This will of God, revealed in the law, is fulfilled by the elect: in the way that was mentioned above: and as God wills it to be done by them. The impious, however, the reprobate, while they act against the doctrine of the law, and thereby against their own duty: they do not act against the absolute, true, and properly so-called will of God: but they are said to act against the will of God for this reason, because they act against that which they know to be pleasing to God, and to be approved by God. But if you object that they therefore do not properly sin, because they do not act against the will of God, which is properly the will of God: that exception is easily refuted. For sin is defined, not as what is a transgression of the secret will and divine good pleasure: but as what is a transgression of the divine law: and what is 1 Jn. 3:4, lawlessness (anomia). For we sin for this reason, because we do not perform the things that are good and pleasing to God, and commanded and owed by us, but the contrary. In the law, however, are manifested: what all men owe to God by duty, and what they do not owe. Therefore, they sin more gravely who act against these things, and are therefore said to sin against the will of God: because they sin against that doctrine by which we are taught what is consistent with the nature of God, and what we owe Him by duty: and what is in itself pleasing and acceptable to God. But if you object again: but God therefore mocks the reprobate: when He commands that they do this or that: if this is not His certain and definite will. He does not mock them at all: because by His law, although He does not reveal what He absolutely wills to be done by them (for this is properly the will of God), yet He clearly teaches what is the duty of Him and of every man. Therefore, the law is deservedly called by Moses, Torah (doctrine): because it teaches everyone what his duty is: adding moreover, that whoever has acted against this duty of his, sins gravely and becomes liable to death. On the contrary, he who has done his duty: him [He rewards]. Lest this seem insufficient to you? Or is this mocking? Tell me, I pray: In the parable of the Gospel, those who were first invited to the wedding, and did not come: was it therefore a mockery to them by the king: because he only signified to them what would be pleasing to him, and what was their duty: and did not command them to be compelled, as the second ones, to come to the wedding? Not at all. Yet meanwhile, the will of the king in inviting the first was not that which it was in the second. For in calling these latter, the will of the king was absolute: that they should come at all, and therefore he also brought it about that they should come at all. To the former, however, he only signified: and that candidly and ingenuously: what would be pleasing to Him. As therefore it cannot be said that He called the first to the wedding with an invitation: although the will of the King was not absolute and simple that they come, as it was in calling the second: so neither can it be said that God mocks the reprobate when He gives them the law and calls them: although it is not His will that they come and obey the law. For it is enough to render them inexcusable: that they understand what things are pleasing to God, and what is their duty what things are pleasing to God, and what is their duty: they would have taken and thought that they were doing it by their own virtue, from God, who has absolute right over them and over all, to be commanded. To that point, that God commanded Abraham to kill his son, when nevertheless He did not want him killed: and to Pharaoh, to let the people go, when nevertheless He did not want them to be let go: and from this many try to gather that there were two, and those contrary, wills in God: one expressed by word, the other hidden in His own mind: We answer that this does not follow at all. For there was only one, and that a constant will: namely, that Abraham’s son was not to be killed: nor was the people to be let go by Pharaoh: and thus both were fulfilled. But as for the command given to Pharaoh, it was a doctrine by which He signified what was to be done by Pharaoh if he did not want to be afflicted by so many plagues: and what was his duty, and in itself just and owed: but it was not a testimony of His absolute will. Wherefore it does not follow from that that there were two wills of God. In the command also given to Abraham, it was not a simple will of God that he should kill his son: but only that he should take the sword, with the intention of killing and sacrificing, and that for the sake of God: and thus show his piety towards God, and his promptness in obeying: which was also entirely done: because this was the will of God. But the will of God did not extend as far as the killing. Therefore, when Abraham, having finished all other things, had extended the sword with which he might slaughter his son: the Lord forbade him to do it. To which will also Abraham complied. Thus neither here was there a double will of God: but one. And the Lord said: offer your son as a burnt offering: this therefore was the will of God: and yet afterwards, He signified another will. It was not another: for He did not first want that it should come to the actual slaughter. Therefore Moses premises, The Lord tempted Abraham: but He only wanted that, with other things actually performed, he should also slaughter him with the promptness of his mind, not with the sword. For this is that which, first and properly, the Lord requires in His precepts: that is, that we should be prompt in mind for His obedience, and by this promptness of our mind of ours, the commandments are properly fulfilled before God. The sum in almost all these arguments is admitted as a parable: for the will of God, properly accepted, is the absolute, certain, and firm decree of God, concerning things to be done, either by Himself or by others: and that this is always fulfilled, and is immutable, we do not doubt to affirm. But the Law and all commandments are called the will of God: because by them it is signified and taught what is in itself just, and pleasing to God: and what is required of us, if we wish to be saved. But alone, it is not properly the will of God: but the Torah, the doctrine of the just: and the command of doing it. But if with this doctrine and command there is joined the decree of God, by which He absolutely wills that what He requires be performed: then it will be said to be properly the will of God: as it is, in so far as it is given to the elect. Wherefore not undeservedly they have distinguished in the schools, not indeed the will of God itself: but the signification of the name of the will of God: in so far as it sometimes signifies the decree of God itself, and the good-pleasure: which is properly called will: whence it is also called the will of good-pleasure, and absolute will, because it is without condition: and most omnipotent, because it is always done. But sometimes it signifies that which is in itself pleasing to God, and just: and which the nature of the divine genius refers to: and which is required of us, if we wish to be saved: which is properly called law, and Torah: whence also will is signified: because by this doctrine it is signified what is pleasing to God, and what is of our duty: And conditional will, because these things are required of us, if we wish to obtain eternal salvation. In truth, however, the will of God, properly accepted, is only one, and that perpetual, and firm: as has now been sufficiently and abundantly declared.

t: But against this it may be objected what St. Peter [and Timothy] says: that He would have all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of his will. (2 Pet. 3 [v. 9]; 1 Tim. 2:4) And therefore either there are diverse and contrary wills in God, or it is his will that all should be saved, but yet are not, because they will not believe. I answer: That the will of God is diversely distinguished by the doctors, as [John] Damascene (The will of God is not diverse, Damascene, bk. 2, ch. 46), into an: 1. Antecedent will 2. Consequent will Lombard and the Schoolmen (bk. 1, ch. 45) into his: 1. Signified will 2. Well-pleasing will Tertullian (Lib. Exhort. ad castitatem.), into his: 1. Efficient will 2. Permissive will Whereof he calls the first voluntas pura and the other voluntas indulgentiae. St. Augustine (Enchiridion, ch. 102 & 103), into his: 1. Effectual working and omnipotent will 2. Not working, or not efficient will Others into his: Absolute will Conditional will Others into his Secret will Revealed will All which, and all such like distinctions of God’s will, if they be diligently observed and well understood, do fall into the same end and do no ways prove either diverse wills to be in God or any contradiction to be in the will of God. For it is most certain that as the essence of God is most simple, without composition or division, so the will of God, which is nothing else but his eternal decree concerning all things, is one and the selfsame immutable and unresistible: in so much that the wicked, who as much as in them lies, do resist the will of God revealed and commanded unto us in his Word, yet notwithstanding, will they, nill they, they fulfill the will of God decreed in Himself from all eternity; as you may see most plainly in the example of Pilate, Herod and the wicked Jews, who in crucifying Christ, rebelled and resisted the will of God revealed in his word, yet herein they did perform the secret will of God, which before all worlds He had determined should be done, as St. Peter shows (Acts 2:23; Augustine in Enchiridion, ch. 98), Et sic in hoc ipso quod contra voluntatem Dei fecerunt, de ipsis facta est voluntas eius: And so in this very thing wherein they did against God’s will, God effected his own will. (Idem, de cor. et gratia) Et de his qui faciunt quod non vult, facit ipse, quae vult: And touching these men which do against his will, He does whatsoever He will.

t: Again, revelation is either uncreated or created. There is an uncreated revelation which is infinite, and such is that which the Father reveals to the Son from all eternity. The created revelation hath three degrees, 1. Imperfect, 2. Perfect, 3. And most perfect. The most perfect revelation is in Christ-man, in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. The perfect revelation is in angels and blessed souls in heaven: the imperfect is in men on earth. The revelation vouchsafed to men on earth is either ineffectual or effectual. The ineffectual is a revelation not available to salvation, such is that revelation which may befall wicked men. For they may prophesy, as is granted, Mt. 7. But I call this revelation ineffectual because they may be castaways for all this. But properly, revelation is the heritage of the saints. For in them only it is effectual, and thus the Lord does grant revelation in two degrees: 1. Sometimes it is such an illumination as works a full assurance: sometimes it is an illumination that works only a persuasion. In weak Christians the work of the Spirit of revelation is persuasion, but in strong Christians it is full assurance.

t: A second question is, How far the Law can draw a sinner to Christ? Antinomians tell us of a legal drawing and conversion, and of an evangelic drawing; the legal drawing they say is ours [that of the reformed]; the latter theirs. Assertion 1. The difference between the letter of the Law and the Gospel is not in the manner of working, for the letter of either Law or Gospel is alike ineffectual and fruitless to draw any to Christ. Christ preached the Gospel to hard-hearted Pharisees; it moved them not. Moses preached the Law and the curses thereof to the stiffnecked Jews and they were as little humbled. Sounds and syllables of ten hells, of twenty heavens and Gospels, without the Spirit’s working, are alike fruitless. And we grant the Law is a sleepy keeper of a captive sinner; he may either steal away from his keeper or if he be awed with his keeper, he is not kept from any spiritual, internal breach of the Law, nor moved thereby to sincere and spiritual walking. But the difference between Law and Gospel is not in the internal manner of working, but in two other things: 1. In the matter contained in Law and Gospel: because nature is refractory to violence and the Law can do nothing but curse sinners; therefore it can draw no man to Christ. The Gospel again contains sweet and glorious promises of giving a new heart to the elect, of admitting to the Prince of peace laden and broken-hearted mourners in Zion and in conferring on them a free imputed righteousness; and this is in itself a taking-way, but without the Gospel-spirit [it is] utterly ineffectual. 2. To the Gospel there is a Spirit added, which works as God does with an omnipotent pull; and this Spirit does also use the Law to prepare and humble; though this be by a higher power than goes along with the Law as the Law.

t: Question 9. Whether every will of God is fulfilled? Denied with a distinction. Answer: Concerning the will properly taken, or of good-pleasure [beneplaciti]: affirmed, Isa. 46:10. Concerning the will taken metonymically, or of command [mandati]: denied. And this opinion is insinuated by Thomas, in [Summa] pt. 1, question 19, article 6, where he disputes that every will of God is always fulfilled, together with article 11, where he distinguishes the will into [the will] of the sign and [the will] of good-pleasure. … Question 11. By what will can anyone justly will that which God does not will? Explained. Answer: We thus explain it: by a right will, which is conformable to the law and general command of God, one can will that which God does not will by the will of good-pleasure, or the hidden [will]. See Gen. 22, compared with Heb. 11:17 and 2 Sam. 7:2-3, 13. Question 12, Whether the precepts of God sometimes differ from his will? Affirmed with a distinction. Answer: In the proximate object they differ: for of the precept, or command, there can be another object—and indeed an opposite one—than [that] of the will or good-pleasure. As is manifest, Gen. 22, where the proximate object of the divine command given to Abraham was the slaying [mactatio] of Isaac; and the object of the good-pleasure, or of the divine will properly so called, was the non-slaying of the same. But although the objects of the will of command and of good-pleasure are opposed among themselves, yet the acts of command and of will are not opposed, but the former is subordinated to the latter. For God, by the will of good-pleasure, willed the command, or to command Abraham; but He did not will the thing commanded to Abraham, or the fulfillment of the commanded thing.

D’Orbel., pt. 1, dist. 46 and many other Scotists, etc. Some answer (as D’Orbellis, etc.) that the voluntas beneplaciti [will of good-pleasure] is ever effectual, but not the voluntas signi; which yet seeing he well explains to be only the making of duty, he might well have said is still effectual to its proper primary effect. Gregory Ariminiensis (and many others) distinguish of the will of complacency and displicency, and that prosecutionis et fugae; and say the latter is effectual and not the former: which others say of the absolute will as distinct from the conditional. The plain truth I have oft opened before: God’s will is the first efficient, the chief dirigent and the final cause (in which the three principles, power, wisdom and goodness are eminent). 1. His efficient will is ever effectual and never frustrated. ‘Whatsoever pleased the Lord (to do) that He did in heaven and in earth, in the sea and in the depths.’ Ps. 135:6. ‘And who has resisted (this) his will?’ Rom. 9:19. 2. His directing will is ever effectual as to the making of the Law or rule, and of due or right thereby: For so far it is efficient of that effect: But it is too oft violated by our sin. 3. His final will or complacency, is God’s being pleased with the being, or action, or relation of the creature, and supposing it, [it] is not efficient [because it is an end, final goal], and therefore [it is] not effectual. t: God’s call sometimes is ineffectual, and sometimes effectual. t: Three things are to be observed in this speech: 1. God’s resolution not always to strive with man by his Spirit. My Spirit has striven a great while; it shall strive yet a little longer; but it shall not strive always. The Holy Spirit is a striving Spirit with the children of men; striving them away from sin, and to bring them to God; striving by the checks of their own consciences, but the ministry of the Word, by the rebukes of Providence; striving by one fair warning after another to reclaim the sinner. Have not we ourselves experienced these strivings?—something within us that has whispered in an hour of temptation, “Do not this abominable thing which the Lord hates?” ‘Twill be our wisdom to hearken to such whispers, and to close with them, striving against sin. Heb 12:4. If the Spirit of God be resisted in its strivings, and quenched in its motions, though it may strive long, yet it will not strive always. ‘Tis a principle with men not to be always persuading those with whom they cannot prevail; neither will the blessed Spirit do so. If Ephraim be joined to idols, is it not a righteous thing with God to say, Strive no more with him, let him alone? Hosea 4:17. What guest will stay long there where he is not welcome? Is it not wisdom then to improve these strivings while we have them? 2. The reason of that resolution: For that he also is flesh; carnal, earthly, sensual, corrupted, depraved, defiled; and therefore ‘tis to no purpose to strive with him; ‘tis but labor lost. It is as good to go about to change the Ethiopian’s skin or the leopard’s spots, as to reclaim and reform these impenitent sinners. Flesh, in scripture, is frequently opposed to spirit. It is the corrupt nature that renders the strivings of the blessed Spirit ineffectual. ‘Tis the law in the members that wars against the law of the mind. Rom. 7:23. The flesh and the spirit are sworn enemies one to another, and between them there is a constant conflict. Gal. 5:17. Now where the flesh, the carnal part, is so far suffered to prevail, as that the man may be denominated flesh, there the Spirit will not always, will not long strive. Those therefore that would enjoy the Spirit’s strivings, must curb and restrain, and not gratify and encourage, the corrupt motions and carnal desires of the flesh and of the mind. Eph. 2:3.

t: 13. In the same way too it cannot be concluded that because the outward calling of the rejected is ineffectual it is therefore not seriously meant by God. Outward calling is always per se [of itself, in principle] a real calling to salvation, since everyone who follows it up thereby gains righteousness in Christ and eternal life: only, in the case of the godless, it is ineffectual because of their hardness of heart. Similarly, the calling from God’s side is always seriously intended, since God promises grace even to the rejected upon condition of faith, and makes faith for them a duty. But of course God omits to give faith to the rejected, because He is not bound to do so in the case of any man… From this it follows that even the calling of the godless is on God’s side ‘sincere and serious’.

t: XXV. Thirdly, it is asked how Christ could offer such prayers to God as openly appear to be repugnant to the divine counsel and will, and thus to the piety and obedience which he most constantly exhibited to the Father? For what? Was he not born and made mediator for this very reason, that he might drink this cup for our salvation? Did he not know that this was the decree of the Father, as he himself testified more than once, that he must suffer many things and be killed? Mt. 16:21. Indeed, when he was being seized by the soldiers, he rebukes Peter for resisting them: “Shall I not drink the cup which my Father hath given me?” How, therefore, is he contrary to himself and to the Father, by requesting with such effort that the cup be transferred from him? Here, indeed, there are many things that can be replied. 1st, We suppose, against the Monothelites, that there was a twofold will in Christ, just as there was a divine and a human nature; these were not indeed adverse and repugnant to one another, but were nevertheless diverse insofar as they were directed toward diverse objects. The divine [will] willed death because it had been so ordained by the Father for our redemption; the human, however, shuddered and prayed against it, because it viewed it as the destruction of nature and the most dire of all evils that could exist; yet the human will is not rightly said to have been repugnant to the divine, because it petitioned not absolutely, but conditionally; not with a deliberate and elective will, but rather with an inefficacious and natural velleity. Therefore, it is to be observed 2nd, that the will can be divided in many ways; for one is called efficacious, another inefficacious; that is called efficacious which is the principle of acting, and which moves and impels a man to execute those things which it wills and to remove, as much as it can, any impediments to operation; [Ineffectual] which is not brought into effect, whether because of impediments arriving from elsewhere, or because it is a simple complacency in the good, or displeasure at evil, and does not proceed further so as to be a principle of operating, nor does it in reality impel one to the execution of the thing, which deserves to be called velleity rather than will. Therefore, when Christ is said to have willed that the cup might pass, this ought not to be understood of an efficacious will which produced in Him any attempt at escaping and extricating Himself from those snares; indeed, we see Him led as a sheep to the slaughter, Isa. LIII:8, so that He in no way resisted, nor attempted to flee from death, but of an ineffectual will which signifies nothing other than a simple displeasure arising from a natural inclination by which the will abhors that which destroys nature. XXVI. The will is either natural and indeliberate, or deliberate and elective. The former is called will by way of nature, the latter by way of reason, thus Thomas, pt. 3, quest. 18, art. 5. Will as nature, or by way of nature, is a physical faculty having a natural inclination toward the preservation of the whole composite, or it is a desire for advantage; it is called indeliberate will because it is borne toward an object considered absolutely without any consideration of circumstances. But will by way of reason is a rational faculty for pursuing the general good of the whole man as he is man, or for following the dictate of the practical intellect advising what is right and just; it is called elective will because it is a desire and affection for justice rather than for one’s own utility; it is also called deliberate will because it regards an object clothed in all its circumstances, and this will is referred to rational cognition as to its cause, because it follows not the instinct of nature but the dictate of reason. The will of nature naturally flees those things which are contrary to nature, such as death, torments, etc. The will by way of reason can be borne even toward those things which are adverse to nature, provided they are just and honorable or necessary; thus, for example, he who by natural will flees and is averse to a bitter potion, nevertheless receives the same by rational will, because he knows there is no other way of recovering health. In the same way, martyrs by nature cannot but shudder at death, but the same persons, nevertheless, approach it eagerly out of reason as the most glorious testimony of the benevolence of God, and glory in it. In clearly the same manner, Christ willed and did not will death, in a different respect. The will by way of nature did not will it, but the same by way of reason willed it; it did not will it insofar as natural appetite was a desire that He might live, and it viewed death absolutely and in itself as the destruction of nature. But insofar as He viewed the same with its circumstances, that is, as decreed by God and necessary for the salvation of the elect, He was borne toward it with a most propense affection, just as He testified elsewhere that this was His food, that He might do the will of His Father. Jn. IV:34; XXVII:4. Will is distinguished into simple and absolute, and hypothetical or conditional. The former is that by which one wills something absolutely and efficaciously, so that he leaves nothing undone so that that will may be brought into effect. The latter in which one wills something under a condition, and which is contained within certain limits. Thus, with an absolute will, the faithful seek the remission of their sins, and whatever things are necessary for their salvation. But with a conditional will, they seek those things which do not pertain to salvation in themselves, nor, whether granted, promote it, or, if denied, remove it—for instance, wealth, health, strength, external peace—in the seeking of which they must always add that condition, expressly or implicitly: “if the will of God so carries it.

t: XXXII. Finally, it is asked here how Christ can be said to have been heard in that prayer from fear, as the apostle testifies, Heb. V:7 [“Who in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death, and was heard in that he feared;”], and elsewhere Christ professes that he is always heard by the Father, Jn. XI:42, when nevertheless death had necessarily to be undergone by him. That which Christ willed simply and absolutely, in that he never suffered a refusal; but that which he willed only under a condition, it is no wonder if he did not obtain it, since that was not so much a will as it was velleity, and that was not so much to be reckoned a rational desire, which ought always to hold the primary place, as a natural inclination and sensitive appetite, which never has the principal role in prayer. 2. Christ was heard from the fear of death, not indeed absolutely, as if He had been freed from the necessity of undergoing death, but in a certain respect, namely, insofar as God, who heard Him, so shook off that fear that He received death most steadfastly and submitted Himself wholly to the divine will, and was thus strengthened so that He laid aside all dread of death. For Christ feared two things above all: 1. Lest He should succumb, overwhelmed by the evils which He saw to be most grievous. 2. Lest He should be swallowed up by death, so that no exit from it would be open. But God heard Him, that is, freed Him from both those fears: 1. Because He so corroborated Him by the power of His Spirit in the midst of the struggle that He most steadfastly and invincibly sustained that most grievous contest. 2. Because He freed Him from death, having loosed the pains of hell by His glorious resurrection; and thus, most truly, in this respect He was heard—not, indeed, that He might not pay the penalty of death, but that He might not be swallowed up by it; not that He might not taste it, but that He might not perish in it; not in the subterfuge of punishments, but in the constant toleration of the same and in a strong and invincible liberation and victory.

t: As God may by metaphor be said to will what by His will, properly speaking, He wills not; so He may by metaphor be said to will what He does will, properly speaking.
